17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the vectors

$$
{c}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 4\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,d=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -11 \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

If ${x}_{1}{c}_{1}+{x}_{2}{c}_{2}=d,$ then what is ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}?$
." :question/worked-solution "If ${x}_{1}{c}_{1}+{x}_{2}{c}_{2}=d,$ then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -11 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 4{x}_{1} \\ 4{x}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -11 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} \\ 4{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} \\ 4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -11 \\ -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=3 \\ 4{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=-11 \\ 4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-5\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the second and the third  equations we get

$$
\begin{aligned}8{x}_{1} & =-16\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${x}_{1}=-2$ into the third equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4(-2)+{x}_{2}=-5\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting ${x}_{1}=-2$ and ${x}_{2}=3$ into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} & =3 \\ (-2)+2(3) & =3 \\ 4 & =3,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives a false statement. 

So, the system has no solution."} {:db/id 17592186342117 :question/id #uuid "eec4fe83-c254-5d51-9484-b88391578898" :question/math-academy-id "q-73952" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186119807 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "92e5e826-3121-500a-9103-e618cb16c5b2" :knowledge-point/title "Solving for Two Coefficients in a Linear Combination"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "32d443f5-4a4c-51aa-af01-414ca3fa7326" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186339577} {:answer/id #uuid "7176331f-77ce-5fd1-a3ac-5da0c1e2a04b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186340136} {:answer/id #uuid "8b60455d-0f91-5c1b-b1a2-179e00d5ba83" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "No solution" :db/id 17592186340376} {:answer/id #uuid "c1c850a2-343b-5521-9ce1-8a561961b355" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186340853} {:answer/id #uuid "f64a326f-5394-5da4-88ca-9fe93d38d48b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186341305}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "32d443f5-4a4c-51aa-af01-414ca3fa7326" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186339577} :answer-field/id #uuid "d05bc05c-9d23-5ddd-9cf1-1346736f76da" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186341745}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the vectors

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ -1 \\ 6\end{aligned}].
$$

If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}=b,$ then what is ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}?$" :question/worked-solution "If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}=b$, then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ -1 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -{x}_{1} \\ 2{x}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2} \\ 3{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ -1 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ -1 \\ 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=-7 \\ -{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=-1 \\ 2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=6\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the first and the second equation we get

$$
-2{x}_{2}=-8\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=4.
$$

Substituting ${x}_{2}=4$ into the first equation yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} & =-7 \\ {x}_{1}-(4) & =-7 \\ {x}_{1} & =-7+4 \\ {x}_{1} & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute ${x}_{1}=-3$ and ${x}_{2}=4$ into the third equation to get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} & =6 \\ 2(-3)+3(4) & =6 \\ 6 & =6,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives a true statement. 

So, the solution of the system is ${x}_{1}=-3$ and ${x}_{2}=4,$ which means

$$
-3{a}_{1}+4{a}_{2}=b.
$$

Consequently, 

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-3+4=1.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186342118 :question/id #uuid "abf235b3-2d59-5bfb-aea0-aa237461f6b8" :question/math-academy-id "q-73954"} {:db/id 17592186342123 :question/id #uuid 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the vectors

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -8 \\ 6\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=b,$ then what is ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}?$" :question/worked-solution "If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=b$, then we have  

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -8 \\ 6\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ -3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 3{x}_{1} \\ -2{x}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{2} \\ -8{x}_{2} \\ 6{x}_{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{3} \\ 5{x}_{3} \\ -3{x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} \\ 3{x}_{1}-8{x}_{2}+5{x}_{3} \\ -2{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=2 \\ 3{x}_{1}-8{x}_{2}+5{x}_{3}=1 \\ -2{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}=2\end{aligned}
$$

We will solve this system using Gaussian elimination. First, we write the augmented matrix for this system:

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & -8 & 5 & 1 \\ -2 & 6 & -3 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Row-reducing the augmented matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & -8 & 5 & 1 \\ -2 & 6 & -3 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -5 \\ -2 & 6 & -3 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=2 \\ {x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=-5 \\ {x}_{3}=6.\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=6.$ Substituting ${x}_{3}=6$ into the second equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{2}-6=-5\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=1.
$$

Now, substituting ${x}_{2}=1$ and ${x}_{3}=6$ into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}-3(1)+2(6)=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-7.
$$

So, the solution of the system is ${x}_{1}=-7$, ${x}_{2}=1$, and ${x}_{3}=6,$ which means 

$$
-7{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}+6{a}_{3}=b.
$$

Consequently, 

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=-7+1+6=0.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186240993 :question/id #uuid "2b7aaa73-fdec-536a-866a-953c6856f39f" :question/math-academy-id "q-105169"} {:db/id 17592186240994 :question/id #uuid 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the vectors

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -10 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=b,$ then what is ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}?$" :question/worked-solution "If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=b$, then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -10 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0 \\ 3{x}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ 0 \\ -{x}_{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{3} \\ 5{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -10 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} \\ 5{x}_{3} \\ 3{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -10 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=-5 \\ 5{x}_{3}=-10 \\ 3{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=1\end{aligned}
$$

We will solve this system using Gaussian elimination. First, we write the augmented matrix for this system:

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 & -10 \\ 3 & -1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Row-reducing the augmented matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 & -10 \\ 3 & -1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 & -10 \\ 0 & 2 & -5 & 16\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & -5 \\ 0 & 2 & -5 & 16 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 & -10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & -5 \\ 0 & 1 & -2.5 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 & -10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :=\frac{1}{5}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & -5 \\ 0 & 1 & -2.5 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=-5 \\ {x}_{2}-2.5\,{x}_{3}=8 \\ {x}_{3}=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=-2.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get 

$$
{x}_{2}-2.5(-2)=8\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=8-5=3.
$$

Finally,  substituting ${x}_{2}=3$ and ${x}_{3}=-2$  into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}-(3)+2(-2)=-5\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2.
$$

So, the solution of the system is ${x}_{1}=2$, ${x}_{2}=3$, and ${x}_{3}=-2,$ which means 

$$
2{a}_{1}+3{a}_{2}-2{a}_{3}=b.
$$

Consequently, 

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=2+3-2=3.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186342130 :question/id #uuid "ff5142a4-ab7b-5300-baa5-14f6253ed7fa" :question/math-academy-id "q-74006"} {:db/id 17592186342132 :question/id #uuid the affirmative case, find the value of $s\cdot t$ from the decomposition $u=sb+tc.$" :question/worked-solution "By definition, $u\in Π$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc & =u \\ s[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4 \\ -3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -7 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}s-2t=3 \\ -s+4t=-7 \\ 3s-3t=3\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ -1 & 4 & -7 \\ 3 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 \\ 3 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & 3 & -6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & -6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}s-2t=3 \\ t=-2 \\ 0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
t=-2.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s-2t & =3 \\ s-2(-2) & =3 \\ s+4 & =3 \\ s & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=-1,\,t=-2,$ we conclude that $u$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
u=-b-2c.
$$

Finally, $s\cdot t=(-1)\cdot (-2)=2.$"} {:db/id 17592186241025 :question/id #uuid "8c4cb4f7-2d57-5ca9-8ffa-a4fe4548b0de" :question/math-academy-id "q-105265"} {:db/id 17592186317208 :question/id #uuid $c=⟨3,-10,2⟩$, and  $u=⟨-2,5,0⟩.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of $s\cdot t$ from the decomposition $u=sb+tc.$" :question/worked-solution "By definition, $u\in Π$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc & =u \\ s[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -10 \\ 2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}s+3t=-2 \\ -4s-10t=5 \\ 2s+2t=0\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -2 \\ -4 & -10 & 5 \\ 2 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 2 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & -4 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The third row of the augmented matrix now corresponds to the equation $0{x}_{1}+0{x}_{2}=-2,$ which has no solution.

So, there are no values of $s$ and $t$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc=u.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $u$ does *not* lie on the plane $Π.$"} {:db/id 17592186403766 :question/id #uuid "da2b75e4-b38a-5b5b-9891-19906308bd00" :question/math-academy-id "q-74600"} {:db/id $$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -2 \\ -6\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 7 \\ 18\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-12 \\ -10 \\ k\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "We know that $b\in \text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ if there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} & =b \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -2 \\ -6\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 7 \\ 18\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-12 \\ -10 \\ k\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{1}+9{x}_{2}=-12 \\ -2{x}_{1}+7{x}_{2}=-10 \\ -6{x}_{1}+18{x}_{2}=k\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}-3 & 9 & -12 \\ -2 & 7 & -10 \\ -6 & 18 & k\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 4 \\ -2 & 7 & -10 \\ -6 & 18 & k\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ -6 & 18 & k\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+6{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & k+24\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The third row of the augmented matrix now corresponds to the equation $0{x}_{1}+0{x}_{2}=k+24.$ Therefore, the system has a solution only if

$$
0=k+24\,⇒\,k=-24.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186241017 :question/id #uuid "4e417e2f-54d8-52fa-a283-38ee2e22e96c" :question/math-academy-id "q-105232"} {:db/id 17592186241019 :question/id #uuid $$

Which of the following vectors could be ${a}_{2}$ if
${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5\end{aligned}]?$" :question/worked-solution "We say that two vectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are *linearly independent* if the only solution to the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}=0
$$

is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ Otherwise, the vectors are *linearly dependent*.

A set containing *only two* vectors is linearly *dependent* if and only if the two vectors are parallel.

From the given options, the correct answer is 

$$
{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 15\end{aligned}].
$$

To see why, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 15\end{aligned}]=-3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5\end{aligned}]=-3{a}_{1}.
$$

This way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3{a}_{1}-3{a}_{1} & =0 \\ 3{a}_{1}+{a}_{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are parallel.

To see why this means that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly dependent, we notice that the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}=0
$$

has the solution ${x}_{1}=3$ and ${x}_{2}=1,$ which is different from ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the set is linearly dependent."} {:db/id 17592186317317 :question/id #uuid 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Consider the following vectors:

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 9 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -12 \\ -4\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Assume that ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}$ are real numbers. Which of the following statements are true?

- The vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},$ and ${a}_{3}$ are linearly dependent.
- The vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},$ and ${a}_{3}$ are linearly independent.
- The equation ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=0$ has only the trivial solution ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$" :question/worked-solution "We say that three vectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},$ and ${v}_{3}$ are *linearly independent* if the only solution to the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}=0
$$

is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$ Otherwise, the vectors are *linearly dependent*.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

The equation ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=0$ corresponds to the system 

$$
{\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+5{x}_{3}=0 \\ 9{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}-12{x}_{3}=0 \\ -2{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system, we create its augmented matrix and reduce it using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 & 5 & 0 \\ 9 & -5 & -12 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, the system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+5{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=0.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}+3(0)=0\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=0
$$

and, substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-3{x}_{1}+2(0)+5(0)=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=0.
$$

Since ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0$, we get that the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ is linearly independent.

Therefore, statements II and III are true, while statement I is false."} {:db/id 17592186241038 :question/id #uuid "81d16fc8-2819-579f-80e6-748f22f14098" :question/math-academy-id "q-105319"} {:db/id 17592186317320 :question/id #uuid "1120ac93-1146-5212-b323-41cae9ac4014" :question/math-academy-id "q-34276" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186119925 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "52a45814-d1e2-5948-b7bd-69dcaf6cd0eb" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Linearly Independent and Dependent Sets Using Row Reduction"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "24069f64-c580-5200-b5e0-1c7ef2ae7e68" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186315321} {:answer/id #uuid "3a15928d-e29a-514a-aa9c-b81e928ccc22" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186315451} {:answer/id #uuid "6b92d802-3085-528a-9c72-efc57cf5c2c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186315724} {:answer/id #uuid "800f5135-a705-5bc5-b182-cd0428d00e1a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "None of the statements are true" :db/id 17592186315821} {:answer/id #uuid "93c3185c-8c40-5110-addf-07d04037df9e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186315941}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "3a15928d-e29a-514a-aa9c-b81e928ccc22" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186315451} :answer-field/id #uuid "22bb0e27-d6d9-5966-9fb5-317681ddbc7c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186316627}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the following vectors:

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Assume that ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}$ are real numbers. Which of the following statements are true?

- The equation ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=0$ has only the trivial solution ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$
- The vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},$ and ${a}_{3}$ are linearly independent.
- The vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},$ and ${a}_{3}$ are linearly dependent." :question/worked-solution "We say that three vectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},$ and ${v}_{3}$ are *linearly independent* if the only solution to the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}=0
$$

is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$ Otherwise, the vectors are *linearly dependent*.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

The equation ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=0$ corresponds to the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0 \\ -3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system, we create its augmented matrix and reduce it using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+5{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we conclude that the basic variables are ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$, while ${x}_{3}$ is the free variable. 

Since there is one free variable, the equation ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=0$ has an infinite number of nonzero solutions, which means that the vectors are linearly dependent.

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Given that $f(x)=(x-2{)}^{2},$ on which of the following intervals is $f(x)$ invertible?

- $x\in (2,\infty )$
- $x\in (-1,5)$
- $x\in (-\infty ,2]$" :question/worked-solution "The graph of the function $f(x)=(x-2{)}^{2},$ can be obtained in the following way:

- Take the curve $y={x}^{2}.$

- Translate it by $2$ units  to  the right  $f(x)=(x-2{)}^{2}.$

![](images/1e/1e3ac550e35a3dc93b3e26e5834f763847b04f5133de02e368124f54dd2b9dd6.png)

A function is invertible on a particular interval if and only if it's a one-to-one function on that interval. To determine the intervals on which the function is invertible, we use the horizontal line test.

- The function $f(x)$ is not invertible on the interval $x\in (-1,5).$ On this interval, some horizontal lines will intersect the curve more than once.

![](images/3e/3ebb316ca122b6786b8ef501fc7c56f8e0e68c8cfc32e5801c493d38382fc26c.png)

- The function $f(x)$ is invertible on the intervals $x\in (2,\infty )$  and $x\in (-\infty ,2].$  On these intervals, any horizontal line will intersect the curve at most once, no matter where we draw the line.

![](images/86/86c7c9cacc7a3868565f33130563ffed0ca423aa087e76cc08d103ea171822ed.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only"."} {:db/id 17592186335899 :question/id #uuid "ffb9d3e2-6b9a-5fb3-b64e-0b7d921759d9" :question/math-academy-id "q-66679" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124474 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "149fa184-850f-52d8-a309-4b79a371a74d" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Intervals on Which a Function is Invertible Given a Description"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "17c1e9df-cdaa-5e98-bb5a-91b82a10bb92" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186333202} {:answer/id #uuid "253331ca-df9d-523a-8811-2487a95d3272" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186333334} {:answer/id #uuid "63786589-d496-56b9-bccb-1a7b14aff44f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186333890} {:answer/id #uuid "9bfaecb8-b49e-5068-aef0-3b70aa437c88" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186334362} {:answer/id #uuid "aa2e9670-55bb-542c-a3ec-ea63c48da4e3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186334478}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "17c1e9df-cdaa-5e98-bb5a-91b82a10bb92" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186333202} :answer-field/id #uuid "5bd33408-f473-5e92-b602-88c8f1b4211b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186335418}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Given that $f(x)=(x-1)^{2}-2,$ on which of the following intervals is $f(x)$ invertible?

- $x\in (-\infty ,1]$
- $x\in (1,\infty )$
- $x\in (-1,3]$" :question/worked-solution "The graph of the function $f(x)=(x-1)^{2}-2$ can be obtained in the following way:

- Take the curve $y={x}^{2}.$

- Translate it by $1$ units to the right,  to get $y=(x-1)^{2}.$

- Finally, translate $y=(x-1)^{2}$  by $2$ units down to get $f(x)=(x-1)^{2}-2.$

![](images/f5/f53a4f97166877085c90acc01e3f8d0c6ac7bb3f704bbfb792d747122d314013.png)

A function is invertible on a particular interval if and only if it's a one-to-one function on that interval. To determine the intervals on which the function is invertible, we use the horizontal line test. 

- The function $f(x)$ is invertible on each of the intervals $x\in (-\infty ,1]$ and $x\in (1,\infty ).$ On these intervals, a horizontal line will intersect the curve at most once, no matter where we draw the line.

![](images/b0/b088c8ed1974a7c259dd54f85aec7a124579981971babfe8dee0313ca23b6458.png)

  

- The function $f(x)$ is not invertible on the interval $x\in (-1,3].$ On this interval, some horizontal lines will intersect the curve more than once.

![](images/b3/b3af13782a01213bb09fdeef38fbeb3fbca3f41348036e6786b4efa74a0166b4.png)

 

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only"."} {:db/id 17592186335901 :question/id #uuid "1120070d-b929-5ac5-a6ba-244a40b57b70" :question/math-academy-id "q-66687"} {:db/id 17592186335903 :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Given that $f(x)=|x-1|-2,$ on which of the following intervals is $f(x)$ invertible?

- $x\in (-\infty ,1]$
- $x\in (1,\infty )$
- $x\in (-\infty ,2]$" :question/worked-solution "The graph of the function $f(x)=|x-1|-2$ can be obtained in the following way:

- Take the curve $y=|x|.$

- Translate it by $1$ units to the right,  to get $y=|x-1|.$

- Finally, translate $y=|x-1|$ by $2$ units down to get $f(x)=|x-1|-2.$

![](images/75/753840da17642582f9dbc0debc18f1fa3efcbbb11142894c1dd823ad6c0c630a.png)

A function is invertible on a particular interval if and only if it's a one-to-one function on that interval. To determine the intervals on which the function is invertible, we use the horizontal line test. 

- The function $f(x)$ is invertible on each of the intervals $x\in (-\infty ,1]$ and $x\in (1,\infty ).$ On these intervals, a horizontal line will intersect the curve at most once, no matter where we draw the line.

![](images/15/15f1c797cbddd2ac8e2e9c5be72f842e7d1accfc5f619af57b1f35a27e1015c0.png)

  

- The function $f(x)$ is not invertible on the interval $x\in (-\infty ,2].$ On this interval, some horizontal lines will intersect the curve more than once.

![](images/a1/a100489b49da7b06c98783b1b1c4ec0de9d891fc2b22f4b36b1a0ac2d54fc4f3.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is "I  and II only"."} {:db/id 17592186335906 :question/id #uuid "7aa0547e-3ef1-575a-ba36-cf93ffa1c8dc" :question/math-academy-id "q-66778"} {:db/id 17592186396687 by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,0)}\frac{{y}^{3}-xy}{{x}^{3}y} & =\frac{{0}^{3}-2(0)}{{2}^{3}(0)} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,0)}\frac{{y}^{3}-xy}{{x}^{3}y} & ={lim}_{x\to (2,0)}\frac{y({y}^{2}-x)}{{x}^{3}y} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,0)}\frac{\cancel{y}({y}^{2}-x)}{{x}^{3}\cancel{y}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,0)}\frac{{y}^{2}-x}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it using direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,0)}\frac{{y}^{2}-x}{{x}^{3}} & =\frac{{0}^{2}-2}{{2}^{3}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{8} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true regarding the limit given below?

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y}
$$

- The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $y=x$
- The limit evaluates to $2$ along the path $y={x}^{2}$
- The limit exists and is equal to $2$" :question/worked-solution "Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y}=\frac{2\cdot {0}^{2}}{2\cdot {0}^{2}-0}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Statement I is true. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=x}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2{x}^{2}}{x(2x-1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2x}{2x-1} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 0}{2\cdot 0-1} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is also true. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y={x}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y={x}^{2}}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y}=\text{DNE}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345005 :question/id #uuid "56c07c72-df51-5ec4-88ac-9185b7690371" :question/math-academy-id "q-74966"} {:db/id 17592186377708 :question/id #uuid "6323a167-9fc1-5848-81f1-63d34a9c63ca" :question/math-academy-id "q-74965" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8958422f-4c02-53af-a3e5-28f8445d5bc0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186377710} {:answer/id #uuid "6f7dc054-8a42-5213-b120-534bafd7ab86" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186377711} {:answer/id #uuid "7ad9cc3c-2948-54af-96ab-97ac3dc5dd75" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186377712} {:answer/id #uuid "de9768d4-de86-55ac-a72b-b0470b48216c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\text{DNE}" :db/id 17592186377713} {:answer/id #uuid "1b2466e9-2081-57a2-b9cc-0260610356d0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186377714}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186377713} :answer-field/id #uuid "f14349ec-0b87-5b7c-b87c-2368f3340f77" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186377709}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "${lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{3}+{y}^{3}}=$" :question/worked-solution "Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{3}+{y}^{3}}=\frac{{0}^{2}\cdot 0}{{0}^{3}+{0}^{3}}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

Let's attempt to evaluate the limit approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths. 

- Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=x}\,\frac{{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{3}+{y}^{3}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}+{x}^{3}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the line $y=2x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=2x}\,\frac{{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{3}+{y}^{3}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}+8{x}^{3}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2}{9} \\  & =\frac{2}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{3}+{y}^{3}}=\text{DNE}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186378636 :question/id #uuid "a45c5a39-df0e-5ca7-830f-279fde3ab785" :question/math-academy-id "q-129403"} {:db/id 17592186380062 :question/id #uuid "eb1f3bd1-4155-5e86-902f-cd91483f7d31" :question/math-academy-id "q-74963"} {:db/id 17592186407847 :question/id #uuid "a9a907de-0404-5ffb-8362-e9676298070b" :question/math-academy-id "q-36139" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "041632fd-d218-5815-9c69-da107f5da160" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186407822} {:answer/id #uuid "091e3fce-c81a-50bf-8d66-819204f1ee13" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186407823} {:answer/id #uuid "4d84526b-47f3-51fb-a168-2cba08c88949" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186407830} {:answer/id #uuid "e7aeae6b-4c5c-573f-8a2d-c1af8e88ebf8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186407840} {:answer/id #uuid "f5036257-dfe1-524a-b3ae-379280f91c23" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186407841}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186407840} :answer-field/id #uuid "1b798538-abe6-5e7d-a0f2-143f5a975750" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186407842}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true regarding the limit given below?

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y={x}^{2}}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+2y} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+2{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{3{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=-{x}^{2}}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+2y} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{-{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+2(-{x}^{2})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{-{x}^{2}}{-{x}^{2}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+2y}=\text{DNE}

{:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "${lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{\sqrt{xy+2}-2}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-4}=$" :question/worked-solution "Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
{lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{\sqrt{xy+2}-2}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-4}=\frac{\sqrt{2\cdot 1+2}-2}{{2}^{2}\cdot {1}^{2}-4}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the numerator: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{\sqrt{xy+2}-2}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-4} & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{(\sqrt{xy+2}-2)(\sqrt{xy+2}+2)}{({x}^{2}{y}^{2}-4)(\sqrt{xy+2}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{(\sqrt{xy+2})^{2}-4}{({x}^{2}{y}^{2}-4)(\sqrt{xy+2}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{xy-2}{(xy-2)(xy+2)(\sqrt{xy+2}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{1}{(xy+2)(\sqrt{xy+2}+2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{1}{(xy+2)(\sqrt{xy+2}+2)} & =\frac{1}{(2\cdot 1+2)(\sqrt{2\cdot 1+2}+2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 4} \\  & =\frac{1}{16}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $\frac{1}{16}.$"} {:db/id 17592186407849 :question/id #uuid "fac05de1-cec1-5741-a5ec-beb8567ada24" :question/math-academy-id "q-129343" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "39f90210-da8d-511b-9d38-b3d158c315d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186407827} {:answer/id #uuid "4005330f-5c8b-5294-9f96-5e9be2626147" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186407828} {:answer/id #uuid "88b04b8f-a6d9-5b86-ba06-a0eb6a004245" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186407833} {:answer/id #uuid "b72aa7bf-e6dc-52f1-8358-bfb499369454" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186407838} {:answer/id #uuid "d17e2afc-964e-5d9b-b663-5d2974b50bec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186407839}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186407828} :answer-field/id #uuid "e093674e-caf5-5f8d-97ff-ca3172fa6889" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186407845}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "${lim}_{x\to (2,1,-1)}\frac{y+z}{\sqrt{x-y}-\sqrt{x+z}}=$" :question/worked-solution "Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,1,-1)}\frac{y+z}{\sqrt{x-y}-\sqrt{x+z}} & =\frac{1+(-1)}{\sqrt{2-1}-\sqrt{2+(-1)}} \\  & =\frac{1-1}{1-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,1,-1)}\frac{y+z}{\sqrt{x-y}-\sqrt{x+z}} & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1,-1)}\frac{(y+z)(\sqrt{x-y}+\sqrt{x+z})}{(\sqrt{x-y}-\sqrt{x+z})(\sqrt{x-y}+\sqrt{x+z})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1,-1)}\frac{(y+z)(\sqrt{x-y}+\sqrt{x+z})}{(x-y)-(x+z)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1,-1)}\frac{(y+z)(\sqrt{x-y}+\sqrt{x+z})}{-(y+z)} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to (2,1,-1)}\frac{\cancel{(y+z)}(\sqrt{x-y}+\sqrt{x+z})}{\cancel{(y+z)}} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to (2,1,-1)}(\sqrt{x-y}+\sqrt{x+z})\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{lim}_{x\to (2,1,-1)}(\sqrt{x-y}+\sqrt{x+z}) & =-(\sqrt{2-1}+\sqrt{2+(-1)}) \\  & =-(1+1) \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $-2.$"} {:db/id 17592186048707} {:db/id 17592186048582 :topic/id #uuid "ab43842c-a68a-5473-977a-14bce3aa134e" :topic/knowledge-points [{:db/id 17592186124542 :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B|C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -5 & 2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 10\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ (shown above) and a basis $C$ of ${R}^{3}.$
The matrix $[T]_{B|C}$ of the linear map $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{3}$ relative to these bases, and the vector $x\in {R}^{2},$ are also given. Find $[T(x)]_{C}.$" :question/worked-solution "We can find the coordinates of the image of $x$ under $T$ relative to the basis $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[T(x)]_{C} & =[T]_{B|C}\cdot [x]_{B}\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to find $[x]_{B},$ the coordinates of $x$ relative to $B.$ So, let

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 10\end{aligned}]={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

This gives us the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-5 \\ 3{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=10.\end{aligned}
$$

We now row-reduce the corresponding augmented matrix using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -5 \\ 3 & -2 & 10\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 \\ 3 & -2 & 10\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -5\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -5\end{aligned}].$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}[T(x)]_{C} & =[T]_{B|C}\cdot [x]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -5 & 2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -10 \\ -10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186395295 :question/id #uuid "473ad29f-d952-5261-9293-cd15e4622b57" :question/math-academy-id "q-97583"} {:db/id 17592186395302 :question/id #uuid :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $G$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ and $$

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It is a type I region, and its type I representation is

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,2\le x\le 4,\,0\le y\le x-2}.
$$

Notice that the left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
y=x-2\,⟹\,x=y+2
$$

and the right boundary of the region is

$$
x=4.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type II region. The type II representation of the region is

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,y-2\le x\le 4},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/57/575e7e482f88635f6267405f66857a5488dac79833fce16d3d998df19e24d119.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{x-2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{y+2}^{4}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}

$$

- The matrix $C$ is not in row echelon form since the leading entry ${c}_{32}\ne 0$ (condition II is violated). 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}5 & 5 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -7 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, only $A$ and $C$ are **not** in row echelon form."} {:db/id 17592186403585 :question/id #uuid "ba6bcd83-87df-5c0b-b121-63a0ff1205ca" :question/math-academy-id "q-72492" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129114 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2d390841-351e-54f5-ad19-90b6ebae5799" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Matrices in Row Echelon Form"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d2449f17-fb24-5f21-b93a-91da7cb73b6f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$A$ and $C$ only" :db/id 17592186403587} {:answer/id #uuid "f82dd2a1-af9f-5176-9521-a602fb86b66c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$A$ only" :db/id 17592186403588} {:answer/id #uuid "a73d0fd1-33f8-5fef-91ee-18ea7bc00233" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$B$ and $C$ only" :db/id 17592186403589} {:answer/id #uuid "1e393d24-d14c-55d4-9c1c-d1fb4487bb44" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$C$ only" :db/id 17592186403590} {:answer/id #uuid "0a24998d-88d6-567d-b060-eecb883f1a8b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$B$ only" :db/id 17592186403591}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "1e393d24-d14c-55d4-9c1c-d1fb4487bb44" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$C$ only" :db/id 17592186403590} :answer-field/id #uuid "80541a17-4cbb-5d55-a794-14a52b470ccb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186403586}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Which of the following matrices are **not** in row echelon form?

$$" :question/worked-solution "Remember that a matrix is in row echelon form if it satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.
- Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The matrix $A$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $B$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $C$ is not in row echelon form since the leading entry ${c}_{22}\ne 0$ (condition II is violated). 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "A statement of the intermediate value theorem is given below but some of its parts are missing.

*Let $f(x)$ be a function that is $\text{ ______ }$ on a closed interval $[a,b].$ If $k$ is a number that lies between $\text{ _________ }$, then there exists a number $c\in [a,b]$ such that $f(c)=k.$*

Going from left to right, in which order should the parts I-III, listed below, be placed into the blank spaces to complete the statement of the theorem?

- continuous
- $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ inclusively
- defined" :question/worked-solution "The intermediate value theorem states the following.

*Let $f(x)$ be a function that is **continuous** on a closed interval $[a,b].$ If $k$ is a number that lies between $f(a)$ **and** $f(b)$ **inclusively**, then there exists a number $c\in [a,b]$ such that $f(c)=k.$*

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II"."} {:db/id 17592186133955 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133477 :question/id #uuid "bb373a5d-aa71-58ed-82e3-b74a8f51d144" 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Suppose that the function $f(x)$ is defined as

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}x+1, & x\le 1 \\ 5-2x, & x>1.\end{aligned}
$$

On which of the following intervals can the intermediate value theorem be applied to the function?" :question/worked-solution "The intermediate value theorem can be applied to closed intervals on which the function is continuous.

The function is discontinuous at $x=1.$ To see this, we note that

$$
{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x)=2\ne 3={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x).
$$

 

We conclude that the intermediate value theorem can be applied to the function $f(x)$ only on closed intervals that do not contain the point $x=1.$ 

From the given options, only the interval $[-2,0]$ is allowed.  The intervals $(1,3]$ and $[-2,1)$ are not closed, $[-2,1]$ and $[0,3]$ contain the point $x=1.$"} {:db/id 17592186048131 :topic/id #uuid "81e52842-e868-5110-93ce-65b6024b5770" :topic/knowledge-points :question/worked-solution "We can classify the equilibrium solutions of an autonomous ODE ${y}^{′}=f(y)$ by examining its phase line.

- An equilibrium solution is a *sink* if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line both point *toward* the equilibrium solution.

- An equilibrium solution is a *source* if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line both point *away* from the equilibrium solution.

- An equilibrium solution is a *node* if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line point in the same direction.

First, we need to find the equilibrium solutions. So, we solve $f(y)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(y) & =0 \\ (y-3)({y}^{2}+3y+9) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equilibrium solution is $y=3.$ 

Now, we analyze the sign of $f(y)$ using a sign table, as follows:

|  | $(-\infty ,3)$ | $(3,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $y-3$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| ${y}^{2}+3y+9$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $f(y)$ | $-$ | $+$ |

So, we have that $f(y)$ is positive for $y\in (3,\infty ),$ and negative for $y\in (-\infty ,3).$

We can now draw the phase line for this equation.

![](images/24/244a46b17ad69e8d7cc3ae4f3d9c3c46c1d6e6a7ea154b849946f8ece6030071.png)

Finally, we classify the equilibrium solution:

- $y=3$ is a source because the nearby solutions diverge away from this point.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$y=3$ is a source"."} {:db/id 17592186362327 :question/id #uuid "e5477d34-1ebb-5af1-ac02-05ea5038d3a0" :question/math-academy-id "q-98762"} {:db/id 17592186362328 17592186045487} :question/problem "The intersection of the planes $x+y-z-3=0$ and $x+2y-3z+18=0$ is given by the line

$$
r(t)=⟨{a}_{1},{a}_{2},0⟩+tb,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Calculate ${a}_{1}+{a}_{2},$ and find a possible direction vector $b.$" :question/worked-solution "We're given that there exists a point on the line where $z=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation gives  

$$
x+y-0-3=0\,⟹\,x=3-y,
$$

and substituting $z=0$ and $x=3-y$ into the second equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(3-y)+2y-3(0)+18 & =0 \\ 3+y+18 & =0 \\ y & =-21.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=3-y=3+21=24$ and $a=⟨24,-21,0⟩$ is a position vector of a point on the line.

Next, we notice:

- For the plane $x+y-z-3=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,1,-1⟩.$

- For the plane $x+2y-3z+18=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,2,-3⟩.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,1,-1⟩\times ⟨1,2,-3⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i+2j+k \\  & =⟨-1,2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the equation of the line is:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+tb \\ r(t) & =⟨24,-21,0⟩+t⟨-1,2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then, ${a}_{1}+{a}_{2}=24-21=3,$ and $b=⟨-1,2,1⟩.$"} {:db/id 17592186338928 :question/id #uuid "b67e5545-6e97-5043-a7bc-c8f5ceaad4b9" :question/math-academy-id "q-71347"} {:db/id 17592186338943 :question/id #uuid "e2974487-1652-5f64-b7d4-0706a72b18a2" :question/math-academy-id "q-71446"} {:db/id 17592186338944 :question/id #uuid "7fd28fdb-4130-5881-857a-aa4f88117872" :question/math-academy-id "q-71447"} {:db/id 17592186366212 :question/id #uuid "56b3e332-cb62-524a-a627-2ac9bac6fdaa" :question/math-academy-id "q-71415"} {:db/id 17592186400429 :question/id #uuid "923148c0-0ecb-5f91-a025-b18771e50157" :question/math-academy-id "q-129224"} {:db/id 17592186421901 :question/id #uuid "3582cc5d-9e46-5e0a-8d0c-b0e74f8f5924" :question/math-academy-id "q-71349" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5a5b51a0-3005-5ddd-b5ab-b8d3b530fe56" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{a}_{2}+{a}_{3}=2,\,b=⟨1,-1,-1⟩" :db/id 17592186421890} {:answer/id #uuid "77d58298-86f5-5da7-a6f5-5aadeb1af6ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{a}_{2}+{a}_{3}=-1,\,b=⟨1,1,-1⟩" :db/id 17592186421891} {:answer/id #uuid "782abb1a-40ca-50f3-9eb2-460b14bea776" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{a}_{2}+{a}_{3}=0,\,b=⟨1,1,-1⟩" :db/id 17592186421892} {:answer/id #uuid "8b4a733d-fbda-5f24-ba39-11bd9f15b6aa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{a}_{2}+{a}_{3}=1,\,b=⟨1,-1,-1⟩" :db/id 17592186421893} {:answer/id #uuid "d67766c9-e639-50ae-a0fa-fe37c24c18e0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{a}_{2}+{a}_{3}=0,\,b=⟨1,-1,-1⟩" :db/id 17592186421896}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186421896} :answer-field/id #uuid "ee9b9e23-e285-51ba-8f2e-0f93320571fc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186421900}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "The intersection of the planes $x+y-1=0$ and $x+z+1=0$ is given by the line

Calculate ${a}_{2}+{a}_{3},$ and find a possible direction vector $b.$" :question/worked-solution "We're given that there exists a point on the line where $x=0.$ Substituting this to the first equation gives

$$
0+y-1=0\,⟹\,y=1,
$$

and substituting $x=0$ into the second equation gives

$$
0+z+1=0\,⟹\,z=-1.
$$

Therefore, $a=⟨0,1,-1⟩$ is a position vector of a point on the line.

Next, we notice:

- For the plane $x+y-1=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $x+z+1=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,1⟩.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}b & ={n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} \\  & =⟨1,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =i-j-k \\  & =⟨1,-1,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The equation of the line is:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+tb \\ r(t) & =⟨0,1,-1⟩+t⟨1,-1,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then, ${a}_{2}+{a}_{3}=1+(-1)=0,$ and $b=⟨1,-1,-1⟩.$"} {:db/id 17592186421902 :question/id #uuid "caefbcdd-6450-5b4b-b965-772f5b87b02a" :question/math-academy-id "q-129208" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0bc5a66d-b1b1-585a-b0bc-21d19ca71687" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{a}_{2}-{a}_{3}=-18,\,b=⟨3,9,-2⟩" :db/id 17592186421889} {:answer/id #uuid "9c3c1355-587b-53a6-a6d7-2db08ae599af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{a}_{2}-{a}_{3}=-20,\,b=⟨3,-2,-9⟩" :db/id 17592186421894} {:answer/id #uuid "d155552d-65e9-593d-bf4d-41010a2e061a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{a}_{2}-{a}_{3}=18,\,b=⟨3,9,-2⟩" :db/id 17592186421895} {:answer/id #uuid "e23fcb96-7207-5675-97d0-1ce03137e6ec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{a}_{2}-{a}_{3}=20,\,b=⟨3,-2,-9⟩" :db/id 17592186421897} {:answer/id #uuid "f9b80375-370c-5de5-b724-efe10f25c766" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{a}_{2}-{a}_{3}=10,\,b=⟨3,-2,-9⟩" :db/id 17592186421898}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186421897} :answer-field/id #uuid "1ea7962c-6925-55c2-86b0-52523c308e6b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186421899}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "The intersection of the planes $2x+3y-3=0$ and $3x+z+19=0$ is given by the line

- For the plane $3x+z+19=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨3,0,1⟩.$

$$
{\begin{aligned}5x-2z+13=0 \\ 2y-3z-25=0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we notice:

- For the plane $5x-2z+13=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨5,0,-2⟩.$

- For the plane $2y-3z-25=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,2,-3⟩.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Given the two planes $x-3y+2z=0$ and $x-2y+5=0$, which of the following statements are true?

- The normal vectors of the planes are parallel.
- The cross product of the normal vectors of the planes is equal to $0.$
- The planes intersect on a line." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that:

- For the plane $x-3y+2z=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,-3,2⟩.$

- For the plane $x-2y+5=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,-2,0⟩.$

Now, let's consider the statements.

- Statements I and II are false. Indeed, computing the cross product of the normal vectors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,-2,1⟩\times ⟨1,-1,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -3 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =4i+2j+k \\  & =⟨4,2,1⟩\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${n}_{1}\times {n}_{2}\ne 0$, the vectors ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are not parallel.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, two non-parallel planes in $3$-dimensional space must intersect on a line.

Therefore, only statement III is true."} {:db/id 17592186263002 :question/id #uuid "d75bf5e3-9255-56f7-a884-2df425d0b593" :question/math-academy-id "q-129258" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186147427 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a19140af-1870-5dee-86a2-6052451803d4" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Intersection of Two Planes"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "10a09fbe-515b-57cf-8dcf-59d4cf635ca0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186260027} {:answer/id #uuid "791d7e03-2398-5d57-a6f1-b2656a2c53dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186260938} {:answer/id #uuid "b85f0f67-a1ad-5f66-89e8-4a14e682bd89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186261492} {:answer/id #uuid "ce5c003d-ae68-5b29-95bb-beffa6bf343e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186261699} {:answer/id #uuid "db417898-4e38-5132-b7f5-64297340a226" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186261812}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "b85f0f67-a1ad-5f66-89e8-4a14e682bd89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186261492} :answer-field/id #uuid "56a5d9fd-3df3-562c-b78d-8959c87ef9de" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186262271}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Given the two planes $x-5y+2z=0$ and $3x-2y+7=0$, which of the following statements are true?

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the parabola shown above?" :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(-1,2),$ and passes through the point $(1,4).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(-1,2),$ and so we have

$$
x+1=2pt,\,y-2=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(1,4),$ we can substitute $x=1$ and $y=4$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
{\begin{aligned}2=2pt \\ 2=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =2pt \\ 1 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{1}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =p{(\frac{1}{p})}^{2} \\ 2 & =p\cdot \frac{1}{{p}^{2}} \\ 2 & =\frac{1}{p} \\ p & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+1=2(\frac{1}{2})t,\,y-2=(\frac{1}{2}){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+1=t,\,y-2=\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186241179 :question/id #uuid "fc08a2c7-414a-5909-a99f-88078655463f" :question/math-academy-id "q-106452" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186157303 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "61e9c047-0bbf-560d-b803-87703164db5b" :knowledge-point/title "Parametrizing a Vertical Parabola"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "197f740e-e51c-586a-9de1-a51303b4bf82" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x+2=5t,\,\,y+3=\frac{5}{2}{t}^{2}" :db/id 17592186238266} {:answer/id #uuid "7cba0acb-f4d5-5356-9aae-f6b41b25e383" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x+2=5t,\,\,y+3=-2{t}^{2}" :db/id 17592186239134} {:answer/id #uuid "7d15632a-23cf-5219-ac0e-c737bf375b1a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x+2=-10t,\,\,y+3=-5{t}^{2}" :db/id 17592186239136} {:answer/id #uuid "dcd090d3-e2a2-5591-b158-3189d26a2627" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x+2=-5t,\,\,y+3=-\frac{5}{2}{t}^{2}" :db/id 17592186239984} {:answer/id #uuid "e08e80c5-bb76-53c3-abae-23501d970ef6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x+2=-\frac{5}{2}t,\,\,y+3=-\frac{5}{2}{t}^{2}" :db/id 17592186240024}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "dcd090d3-e2a2-5591-b158-3189d26a2627" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "x+2=-5t,\,\,y+3=-\frac{5}{2}{t}^{2}" :db/id 17592186239984} :answer-field/id #uuid "3381ca1b-3b5a-5935-a443-b7a1f878342b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186240426}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "![](images/0c/0c37bb9e010bdb19de2afc8707b6cf1cef69638c9f4721c407c1593f3a387b87.png)

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(-2,3),$ and so we have

$$
x+2=p{t}^{2},\,y-3=2pt.
$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}8=p{t}^{2} \\ 8=2pt.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}8 & =2pt \\ 4 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{4}{p}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
x+2=(2){t}^{2},\,y-3=2(2)t,

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(2,-5),$ and so we have

$$
x-2=p{t}^{2},\,y+5=2pt.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(-10,7),$ we can substitute $x=-10$ and $y=7$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
{\begin{aligned}-12=p{t}^{2} \\ 12=2pt.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}12 & =2pt \\ 6 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{6}{p}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}-12 & =p{(\frac{6}{p})}^{2} \\ -12 & =p\cdot \frac{36}{{p}^{2}} \\ -12 & =\frac{36}{p} \\ p & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-2=(-3){t}^{2},\,y+5=2(-3)t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-2=-3{t}^{2},\,y+5=-6t.

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & =2pt \\ t & =-\frac{1}{2p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the first equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =p{(-\frac{1}{2p})}^{2} \\ 1 & =p\cdot \frac{1}{4{p}^{2}} \\ 1 & =\frac{1}{4p} \\ p & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-1=(\frac{1}{4}){t}^{2},\,y+3=2(\frac{1}{4})t,
$$

$$

What is the probability of choosing a red card within the first $5$ tries? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "A geometric random variable $X$ with probability of success $p$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(1-p)^{x-1}p
$$

Let $X$ be the number of cards picked until a red one is chosen. Since there are $26$ red cards in a $52$ cards deck, the chance of choosing a red card is $\frac{26}{52}.$ Thus, the number of chosen cards before getting a red card can be modeled as a geometric random variable with a probability of success

$$
p=\frac{26}{52}=\frac{1}{2}=0.5.
$$

So, $X∼\text{Geom}(0.5).$ In this case, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(1-0.5)^{x-1}(0.5) \\  & =(0.5)^{x-1}(0.5)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability of choosing a red card within the first $5$ tries is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 5) & =P(X\in {1,2,3,4,5}) \\  & =f(1)+f(2)+f(3)+f(4)+f(5) \\  & =(0.5)^{1-1}(0.5)+(0.5)^{2-1}(0.5)+(0.5)^{3-1}(0.5)+(0.5)^{4-1}(0.5)+(0.5)^{5-1}(0.5) \\  & =(0.5)+(0.5)(0.5)+(0.5)^{2}(0.5)+(0.5)^{3}(0.5)+(0.5)^{4}(0.5) \\  & =[1+0.5+(0.5)^{2}+(0.5)^{3}+(0.5)^{4}](0.5) \\  & ≈0.969\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186265977 :question/id #uuid "88e110e9-1d53-54ee-a4b5-ea24d610dbe0" :question/math-academy-id "q-130789"} {:db/id 17592186305023 :question/id #uuid Given the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ above for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y,$ calculate $P(Y<2).$" :question/worked-solution "If the random variables $X$ and $Y$ have joint distribution with joint probability mass function $f(x,y),$ then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & ={f}_{X}(x)={\sum }_{y}f(x,y) \\ P(Y=y) & ={f}_{Y}(y)={\sum }_{x}f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

In this case, the marginal distribution for $X$ corresponds to the row totals, and the marginal distribution for $Y$ corresponds to the column totals. Let's add these row and column totals to our table:

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $\frac{3}{7}$ | $\frac{1}{7}$ | $\frac{4}{7}$ |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{2}{7}$ | $\frac{1}{7}$ | $\frac{3}{7}$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $\frac{5}{7}$ | $\frac{2}{7}$ | $1$ |

The marginal mass function for $Y$ is given in the following table:

| $y$ | $1$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}_{Y}(y)$ | $\frac{5}{7}$ | $\frac{2}{7}$ |

Finally, using the table of values of the marginal mass function for $Y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<2) & =P(Y\in {1}) \\  & =P(Y=1) \\  & =\frac{5}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186272363 :question/id #uuid "c3e212fb-b000-51c0-9b9c-560a14885036" :question/math-academy-id "q-142714"} {:db/id 17592186272364 :question/id #uuid "4d18fe4f-c908-58f7-9a78-04f4bc6d6db6" :question/math-academy-id "q-142718" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186162072 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "96473ec4-67f8-5614-b187-0961062aac29" :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Cumulative Probability Given a Joint Distribution"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4b199b00-2e32-51b7-a0a2-2af7edc30793" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.6" :db/id 17592186269945} {:answer/id #uuid "a48bdf26-5f1a-5acc-91d7-652daba55fb1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.45" :db/id 17592186270736} {:answer/id #uuid "aa7ab526-7b74-5841-a507-644509a22dcc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.5" :db/id 17592186270792} {:answer/id #uuid "e233ef36-ef94-5e6c-895a-e363b992f2f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.65" :db/id 17592186271256} {:answer/id #uuid "e984de61-29d8-5c1f-b4c2-570abff33fd7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.4" :db/id 17592186271313}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "e233ef36-ef94-5e6c-895a-e363b992f2f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.65" :db/id 17592186271256} :answer-field/id #uuid "7c1240f6-22a0-5c0f-bdb8-d662a62e2820" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186271728}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "| $f$ | $Y=-1$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ |

Given the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ above for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y,$ calculate $P(|Y|>0).$" :question/worked-solution "If the random variables $X$ and $Y$ have joint distribution with joint probability mass function $f(x,y),$ then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & ={f}_{X}(x)={\sum }_{y}f(x,y) \\ P(Y=y) & ={f}_{Y}(y)={\sum }_{x}f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

In this case, the marginal distribution for $X$ corresponds to the row totals, and the marginal distribution for $Y$ corresponds to the column totals. Let's add these row and column totals to our table:

| $f$ | $Y=-1$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.15$ | $0.1$ | $0.3$ | $0.55$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.05$ | $0.25$ | $0.15$ | $0.45$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.2$ | $0.35$ | $0.45$ | $1$ |

The marginal mass function for $Y$ is given in the following table:

| $y$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}_{Y}(y)$ | $0.2$ | $0.35$ | $0.45$ |

Finally, using the table of values of the marginal mass function for $Y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|Y|>0) & =P(Y\in {-1,1}) \\  & =P(Y=-1)+P(Y=1) \\  & =0.2+0.45 \\  & =0.65.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186272365 :question/id #uuid "631b8eef-33a2-5446-80b6-ad61831c34a2" :question/math-academy-id "q-142723"} {:db/id 17592186162102 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id | $X=3$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ | $0.05$ |
| $X=6$ | $0.25$ | $0$ | $0.1$ |
| $X=9$ | $0$ | $0.1$ | $0.1$ |

Compute $P(0<X\le 6\,|\,Y=3)$ given that the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above." :question/worked-solution "By the multiplication law for conditional probability, the required conditional probability is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0<X\le 6\,|\,Y=3) & =\frac{P((0<X\le 6),Y=3)}{P(Y=3)} \\  & =\frac{P(X=3,Y=3)+P(X=6,Y=3)}{P(Y=3)} \\  & =\frac{f(3,3)+f(6,3)}{{f}_{Y}(3)},\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the marginal distribution of $Y.$

Recall that the marginal distribution for $Y$ corresponds to the column totals. Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(3) & =f(0,3)+f(3,3)+f(6,3)+f(9,3) \\  & =0+0.1+0+0.1 \\  & =0.2.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given table, we have that $f(3,3)=0.1$ and $f(6,3)=0.$ 

Finally, substituting our values into our formula above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0<X\le 6\,|\,Y=3) & =\frac{f(3,3)+f(6,3)}{{f}_{Y}(3)} \\  & =\frac{0.1+0}{0.2} \\  & =\frac{0.1}{0.2} \\  & =0.5.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186162104 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161670 :question/id #uuid "2afabb9d-bd38-50f1-9afd-710ab839163c" :question/math-academy-id "e-10049"} :knowledge-point/id A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 7 & 4 \\ 3 & 6 & 3\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

By applying elementary column operations of the form ${C}_{i}:={C}_{i}+k{C}_{1},$ the matrix $A$ can be transformed into the matrix $B.$ What are the elementary column operations?" :question/worked-solution "To transform $A$ into $B,$ we need to make entries to the right of ${a}_{31}=3$ equal to $0.$

To do this, we can apply the following elementary column operations:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 7 & 4 \\ 3 & 6 & 3\end{aligned}] &  & \,\begin{aligned}{C}_{2}:={C}_{2}-2{C}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & 4 \\ 3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] &  & \,\begin{aligned}{C}_{3}:={C}_{3}-{C}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =B\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the elementary column operations are

$Y$ are shown below. Given that the corresponding joint probability mass function is $f(x,y),$ find $f(3,1).$

| | $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}_{X}(x)$ | $0.2$ | $0.3$ | $0.5$ | |  | | $y$ | $1$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}_{Y}(y)$ | $0.25$ | $0.75$ | |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| ${f}_{X}(x)$ | $0.2$ | $0.3$ | $0.5$ |
| $y$ | $1$ | $2$ |  |
| ${f}_{Y}(y)$ | $0.25$ | $0.75$ |  |" :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "Two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Therefore, since our discrete random variables are independent, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3,1) & ={f}_{X}(3)\cdot {f}_{Y}(1) \\  & =0.5\cdot 0.25 \\  & =0.125.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186162305 :question/id #uuid "ef7189f8-0543-59c5-b47f-ffb206830ccd" :question/math-academy-id "q-110386"} {:db/id 17592186275113 :question/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "For a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ where $n$ is the number of trials, and $p$ is the probability of success on each trial,  we have the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x}
$$

Here, we have $X∼B(6,0.2),$ so $X$ has the probability mass function

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{x})(0.2)^{x}(0.8)^{6-x}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(3\le X\le 5) & =P(X\in {3,4,5}) \\  & =f(3)+f(4)+f(5) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{3})(0.2)^{3}(0.8)^{6-3}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{4})(0.2)^{4}(0.8)^{6-4}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{5})(0.2)^{5}(0.8)^{6-5} \\  & =20(0.2)^{3}(0.8)^{3}+15(0.2)^{4}(0.8)^{2}+6(0.2)^{5}(0.8) \\  & ≈0.0988\end{aligned}
$$

to $4$ decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186265794 :question/id #uuid "e0316062-8105-57c8-93fe-257f0fc7faf0" :question/math-academy-id "q-129973"} {:db/id 17592186295112 :question/id #uuid :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Given that $X∼B(7,0.5),$ compute $P(X\le 6).$ Round your final answer to $4$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "For a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ we have the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x}
$$

Here, we have $X∼B(7,0.5),$ so $X$ has the probability mass function

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{x})(0.5)^{x}(0.5)^{7-x}.
$$

Computing $P(X\le 6)$ will require us to compute $f(x)$ at $x=0,1,2,…,6.$ However, if we compute the complement $P(X>6)$ instead, then we will only have to compute $f(x)$ at $x=7,$ which will result in a much faster computation.

Computing $P(X>6),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>6) & =P(X\in {7}) \\  & =f(7) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{7})(0.5)^{7}(0.5)^{7-7} \\  & =(0.5)^{7} \\  & ≈0.0078\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 6) & =1-P(X>6) \\  & ≈1-0.0078 \\  & =0.9922\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186048485} {:db/id 17592186048750} {:db/id 17592186049014} {:db/id 17592186049632} {:db/id 17592186166827 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Given $X∼\text{Geom}(\frac{3}{5}),$ compute $P(X\ge 5).$" :question/worked-solution "If $X∼\text{Geom}(p),$ then $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}(1-p)^{x-1}p, & x=1,2,3,… \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Here, $X∼\text{Geom}(\frac{3}{5}),$ so the distribution of $X$ in this case is

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}{(\frac{2}{5})}^{x-1}(\frac{3}{5}), & x=1,2,3… \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

There are infinitely many values of $X$ such that $X\ge 5.$ However, we can simplify the computation by using the complement instead:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 5) & =1-P(X<5)\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the complement, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<5) & =P(X\in {1,2,3,4}) \\  & =P(X=1)+P(X=2)+P(X=3)+P(X=4) \\  & =f(1)+f(2)+f(3)+f(4) \\  & ={(\frac{2}{5})}^{0}(\frac{3}{5})+{(\frac{2}{5})}^{1}(\frac{3}{5})+{(\frac{2}{5})}^{2}(\frac{3}{5})+{(\frac{2}{5})}^{3}(\frac{3}{5}) \\  & =0.9744.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 5) & =1-P(X<5) \\  & =1-0.9744 \\  & =0.0256.\end{aligned}

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}(1-p)^{x-1}p, & x=1,2,3,… \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Here, $X∼\text{Geom}(\frac{2}{3}),$ so the distribution of $X$ in this case is

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x-1}(\frac{2}{3}), & x=1,2,3… \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

There are infinitely many values of $X$ such that $X\ge 6.$ However, we can simplify the computation by using the complement instead:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 6) & =1-P(X<6)\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the complement, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<6) & =P(X\in {1,2,3,4,5}) \\  & =P(X=1)+P(X=2)+P(X=3)+P(X=4)+P(X=5) \\  & =f(1)+f(2)+f(3)+f(4)+f(5) \\  & ={(\frac{1}{3})}^{0}(\frac{2}{3})+{(\frac{1}{3})}^{1}(\frac{2}{3})+{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}(\frac{2}{3})+{(\frac{1}{3})}^{3}(\frac{2}{3})+{(\frac{1}{3})}^{4}(\frac{2}{3}) \\  & ≈0.9959.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 6) & =1-P(X<6) \\  & ≈1-0.9959 \\  & =0.0041.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186265861 :question/id #uuid "112e5117-a921-5aad-a945-7d294eb35ece" :question/math-academy-id "q-130239"} {:db/id 17592186360763 :question/id #uuid 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Determine the value of $(\frac{6}{2}).$" :question/worked-solution "The binomial coefficient $(\frac{n}{r})$ is given by the formula

$$
(\frac{n}{r})=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!}.
$$

In this case, we have $n=6$ and $r=2.$ Therefore,

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true regarding the function $y=tan⁡x?$ Assume that $n$ is an integer.

- The domain of the function is all real numbers except $x=\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi $
- The function has zeros at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi $ for any integer $n$
- The range of the function is $y\in (-\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4})$" :question/worked-solution "Let's plot the graph of $y=tan⁡x.$

![](images/73/732955302ca49a41f6c43cf242d7c869e630e88d804c4b56a5beb3b081f2d230.png)

Let's go through each statement.

- Statement I is true. The function is defined everywhere, except where $x=\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi .$

- Statement II is false. The zeros occur at $x=0,\pm \pi ,\pm 2\pi ,…,$ which can be written as $x=n\pi .$

- Statement III is false. The function takes values on all the real numbers, hence the range is $y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

So, the correct answer is "I only"."} {:db/id 17592186237989 :question/id #uuid "6f5925ee-40c3-50af-9950-ecf1ea188724" :question/math-academy-id "q-103295"} {:db/id 17592186297168 :question/id #uuid - The function has asymptotes at $x=n\pi .$
- $tan⁡(x)=tan⁡(x+2n\pi ).$
- The range of the function is $[-1,1].$" :question/worked-solution "Let's recall the graph of $y=tan⁡x.$

![](images/31/31b430f003171dcc04a8f17402d6035fbbc305c244d3676bbf5da83fa447bd50.png)

Let's examine each statement.

- Statement I is false. The function $y=tan⁡x$ has asymptotes at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi n.$

- Statement II is true. The function has period $\pi .$ So, $tan⁡(x+2n\pi )=tan⁡(x+n\pi +n\pi )=tan⁡(x+n\pi )=tan⁡(x).$

- Statement III is false. The range of $y=tan⁡x$ is $(-\infty ,+\infty ).$"} {:db/id 17592186176050 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175696 :question/id #uuid "f4649856-d777-5468-a7f4-df50479e36d7"
