\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x
$$

If the integrand $f(x)$ is continuous on $(-\infty, \infty),$ then we can break the integral up into two improper integrals, each with a single unbounded endpoint:

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = \int_{-\infty}^{0} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x + \int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x
$$

Then, we can compute each of the two integrals separately and combine their results. 

**Watch out!** If either of the two integrals on the right-hand side is divergent, then the integral on the left-hand side is also divergent." :tutorial/id #uuid "b58359c2-9f54-5bd7-8005-df9313559853" :tutorial/math-academy-id 932 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e2a6a97c-d17d-5e17-9d7b-d0d1dbe224ca" :step/math-academy-id 618349 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106953}} {:db/id 17592186107173 :tutorial/content "Consider an improper integral in which both the left and right endpoints are unbounded:

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = \int_{-\infty}^{0} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x + \int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x
$$

Evaluating two improper integrals can be quite time-consuming. However, we can shorten the process if we see that $f(x)$ is an even or odd function. 

- Recall that $f(x)$ is an even function if $f(-x) = f(x).$ Even functions are symmetrical about the $y$-axis. Therefore, if $f(x)$ is even, we have

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{0} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = \int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x,
$$

provided that the integrals are convergent. Moreover, if $f(x)$ is even and the above integrals are convergent, then

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = 2\int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

- Recall that $f(x)$ is an odd function if $f(-x) = -f(x).$ Therefore, if $f(x)$ is odd, we have

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{0} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = -\int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x,
$$

provided that the integrals are convergent. Moreover, if $f(x)$ is odd and the above integrals are convergent, then

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = 0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "04e63304-93d0-5edd-985c-6a732614917f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4359 :tutorial/title "Improper Integrals of Even and Odd Functions"} :step/id #uuid "4ed58d6e-1526-5297-982b-b32247e84e4b" :step/math-academy-id 618353 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106955}} {:db/id 17592186107099 :tutorial/content "Computing the definite integral of a function over the entire real line requires us to break the integral into two parts and separately evaluate each one.

:topic/math-academy-id 1262} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186101837 :step/content {:db/id 17592186101931 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to compute $\lim\limits_{x \to \, 1} f(x)$ for the piecewise function $f(x)$ given below.

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}\, & \text{ for }\,x<1 \\ 2\, & \text{ for }\,x=1 \\ -(x-1)^{3}+3\, & \text{ for }\,x>1\end{aligned}
$$

We begin by sketching a graph of the function:

![](images/01/01e1704152432a01a1491f6d7575ada56907272e53f5eeee8a90b8bc96f3eb51.png)

To compute $\lim\limits_{x \to \, 1} f(x),$ we must compute the left and right-sided limits separately.

- Approaching from the left, we have $x<1,$ so we use the expression $f(x) = x^3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{-}}{x}^{3} \\  & ={1}^{3} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Approaching from the right, we have $x>1,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=-(x-1)^3+3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{+}}-(x-1)^{3}+3 \\  & =-(1-1)^{3}+3 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Because the left and right-sided limits are not equal, the overall limit does not exist: 

$$
\lim\limits_{x \to \, 1} f(x) = \text{DNE}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "80db4900-d9c5-5900-b975-5c26b8f713e2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 236 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d1483e1b-2de0-5e5b-a8d1-f4d81897891d" :step/math-academy-id 424 :step/next {:db/id 17592186101838}} {:db/id 17592186101838 :step/content {:db/id 17592186100977 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186100753 :question/id #uuid "62d73be9-5f67-5f44-a45a-f5c25a4dfe27" :question/math-academy-id "e-64"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0995bfd4-20b1-5f12-9d1d-fcb180a6291e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049534} {:db/id 17592186050454}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186101393} {:db/id 17592186101394} {:db/id 17592186233894} {:db/id 17592186234002} {:db/id 17592186314839} {:db/id 17592186323844} {:db/id 17592186323846} {:db/id 17592186362398}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the One-Sided Limits of a Piecewise Function when the Limits Coincide"} :step/id #uuid "51e2792d-7ab3-57f6-a8aa-4475d65fedf7" :step/math-academy-id 425 :step/next {:db/id 17592186101839}} {:db/id 17592186101839 :step/content {:db/id 17592186100978 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186100754 :question/id #uuid "e9a033d1-eb3f-5e7e-8237-346b03681499" :question/math-academy-id "e-65"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "bdd4a2e4-b0e6-54e8-972c-3dc194ce4ab3" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186101395} {:db/id 17592186101396} {:db/id 17592186234003} {:db/id 17592186234004} {:db/id 17592186297268} {:db/id 17592186314882} {:db/id 17592186314883} {:db/id 17592186323847} {:db/id 17592186323859} {:db/id 17592186392101}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the One-Sided Limits of a Piecewise Function when the Limits Do Not Coincide"} :step/id #uuid "e1dad1df-a9ec-5939-84eb-1443d3e7f165" :step/math-academy-id 428 :step/next {:db/id 17592186101840}} {:db/id 17592186101840 :step/content {:db/id 17592186101932 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 0}f(x)$ for the piecewise function given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x)={\begin{aligned}{3}^{x+1}\, & \text{ for }\,x<0 \\ \sqrt{{x}^{2}+9}\, & \text{ for }\,x\ge 0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

To get an idea of the behavior of the function around $x=0,$ we can plot the function.

![](images/78/78a832c65a4bb5862694717f52704a61660bd81a34eb7a72cfeeb98a52bb50f1.png)

To compute $\lim\limits_{x \to \, 0} f(x),$ we must compute the left and right-sided limits separately.

- Approaching from the left, we have $x < 0,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=3^{x+1}.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}{3}^{x+1} \\  & ={3}^{0+1} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

- Approaching from the right, we have $x>0,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=\sqrt {x^2+9}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+9} \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+9} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

The left and right-sided limits both exist and are equal. So, the overall limit is

$$
\lim\limits_{x \to \, 0} f(x) =3.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "416b850c-1c8d-5794-a787-3a59d48d0616" :tutorial/math-academy-id 239 :tutorial/title "Limits of Piecewise Functions"} :step/id #uuid "f2bafd4a-88b6-500a-b45d-6de37cdf6804" $$

![](images/67/673ea82819858b9a46e0e351a8d6f41b069ed039ee0d31a382110f938f7ef72a.svg)

We can reduce $M$ to row echelon form using the standard Gaussian elimination algorithm. The algorithm that we use is very similar to the case of $2 \times 2$ systems. 

Our goal is to create a descending "staircase" of $1$'s with $0$'s below, and we achieve this using elementary row operations. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & 0 & -6 & -24\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{6}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix is now in row echelon form, and we can apply back substitution to solve the original system of equations.

**Note:** The row echelon form of a matrix is *not* unique.  In the previous example, after the second row operation we arrived at

![](images/35/35627a034b30736abb057c01f3251fc047dce780a8cbcf389f8b5c2c2317d766.svg)

This augmented matrix is already in row echelon form! However, it is always useful to do an extra step and obtain $1$'s along the main diagonal, like we did previously:

![](images/32/32a252e05e299a206f2f3776a2a04419f21726e1f8f542cfd4f328dac3251f21.svg)

Having $1$'s along the main diagonal makes the final back substitution process a little easier." :tutorial/id #uuid "5d8cb1c1-9e09-560f-83ad-7c8a3d0a78cc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3155 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "54dae6c6-bb01-588b-b012-dc097a5b2c65" :step/math-academy-id 17196 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097519}} {:db/id 17592186097519 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097842 :tutorial/content "The **standard Gaussian elimination** for a $3 \times 3$ system can be described as follows:

- If $a_{11} \neq 0$ and $a_{11} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_1:=R_1/a_{11}.$

- We use first row and the necessary row operations to make the remaining entries of the first column below $a_{11}$ equal to $0.$ Namely, 

- if $a_{21} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_2:=R_2 + (-a_{21})R_1;$

- if $a_{31} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{31})R_1.$

- If $a_{22} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_2:=R_2/a_{22}.$

- We use the second row and the necessary row operation to make the entry below $a_{22}$ equal to $0.$ Namely, 

- if $a_{32} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{32})R_2.$

- If $a_{33} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3/a_{33}.$

- In some exceptional cases, such as when the element on the diagonal is equal to $0,$ we first need to exchange rows. Then proceed using the same steps as above.

Carrying out the above algorithm will convert the matrix to row echelon form." :tutorial/id #uuid "955c2b9a-3d5f-52c3-b4f3-62541732ffcc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3156 :tutorial/title "General :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to solve the equation

$$
\sec x={\sqrt{2}}, \qquad  0^\circ\leq x <   360^\circ.
$$

Most calculators don't have a $\textrm{arcsec}{x}$ button, so we can't get a principal value immediately. However, by rewriting the equation in terms of $\cos{x}$, we can get a principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sec}x & =\sqrt{2} \\ \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}x} & =\sqrt{2} \\ \operatorname{cos}x & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can proceed as usual. Our principal value is

$$
x = \arccos \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right)= 45^\circ.
$$

Since $45^\circ$ lies inside the required domain, our first solution is $x_1=45^\circ.$ It lies in the first quadrant and has a reference angle $\theta_R = 45^\circ.$

Since $\cos{x} > 0,$ the second solution must lie in the fourth quadrant, and it also has a reference angle $\theta_R = 45^\circ.$

![](images/c7/c722d4fa2b77011e4df5b086c19bb09943446941484cfaf87559ca39a52183bc.png)

Since the second solution $x_2$ lies in the $4$th quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
x_2 = 360^\circ - 45^\circ = 315^\circ .
$$

So, the solutions are $x=45^\circ, 315^\circ.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "0fd2eba9-8794-5210-bea2-d726a0af4875" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2564 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "646dc860-2777-5e44-aa90-555d9b22ef5e" :step/math-academy-id 11842 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116025}} {:db/id 17592186116025 :step/content {:db/id 17592186115179 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186115008 :question/id #uuid "0d6c1aa8-a2d1-5104-8e27-686c7dd16808" :question/math-academy-id "e-3527"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ec3e2ddd-4937-5837-a03a-b7568bff9b87" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049568} {:db/id 17592186050928}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186115611} {:db/id 17592186115615} {:db/id 17592186292786} {:db/id 17592186297221} {:db/id 17592186297223} {:db/id 17592186297227} {:db/id 17592186345226}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Trigonometric Equation Involving Secant with Special Angles"} :step/id #uuid "f3690006-d413-5d43-b44b-7db5a3b33035" :step/math-academy-id 11843 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116089}} {:db/id 17592186116026 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116464 :tutorial/content "We can solve an equation involving secant over any desired domain. For example, suppose that we want to solve the equation

$$
\sec x = 2, \qquad -2\pi < x \leq 2\pi.
$$

We can proceed as usual. Recall that $\sec x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}.$ Therefore, the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\cos x = \dfrac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, we find the principal value:

$$
x = \arccos \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \right)= \dfrac{\pi}{3}
$$

Since $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ lies inside the required domain, our first solution is ${\color{red}x_1}=\dfrac{\pi}{3}.$ It is in the first quadrant and has a reference angle $\theta_R = \dfrac{\pi}{3}.$

Since $\cos{x} > 0,$ the second solution must lie in the fourth quadrant, and it also has a reference angle $\theta_R = \dfrac{\pi}{3}.$

![](images/31/318eba038feb091d6e3adb80ddf325de6039bb331a7713cf1e2c02171a6388d4.png)

Since the second solution $\color{blue}x_2$ lies in the $4$th quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
{\color{blue}x_2} = 2\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{5\pi}{3}
$$

However, we're not done yet. The domain $-2\pi < x \leq 2\pi$ is larger than one period, so there are more than two solutions.

To get the remaining solutions in the desired domain, we need to find angles that are coterminal with ${\color{red}x_1}$ or ${\color{blue}x_2}.$ So, we subtract integer multiples of $2\pi$ until all possible solutions are found:

$$
\eqalign{
x_3 & = {\color{red}x_1} -2\pi = \dfrac{\pi}{3}- 2\pi= -\dfrac{5\pi}{3},\
x_4 &= {\color{blue}x_2} -2\pi = \dfrac{5\pi}{3}- 2\pi= -\dfrac{\pi}{3}.}
$$

Adding or subtracting any more multiples of $2\pi$ would result in solutions outside the desired domain. So, we have found all the solutions.

Therefore, the solutions are  $x = \pm \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \pm \dfrac{5\pi}{3}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b5492203-ceec-581f-aede-beedabd8c432" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2565 :tutorial/title "Solving a solutions to the equation

$$
\sec{x} = \dfrac{1}{5}, \qquad  0 \leq x < 2\pi?
$$

Recall that $\sec{x}= \dfrac{1}{\cos{x}}.$ Therefore, the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\cos{x} = 5.
$$

This equation has no solution because we always have $-1 \leq \cos{x} \leq 1,$ and the number $5$ is outside of this range. Therefore, $\sec{x} = \dfrac{1}{5}$ has no solution.

In general, when $-1 < a < 1,$ there are no values of $x$ such that $\sec x = a.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "d03c5da6-6a4c-543e-96e9-e7ff27b4ce2c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2896 :tutorial/title "Equations Involving the Secant Function With No Solutions"} :step/id #uuid "9465725a-2525-53da-934d-4381143156f7" :step/math-academy-id 15616 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116028}}] :activity/title "Elementary Trigonometric Equations Containing Secant" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186115411} {:db/id 17592186116024 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116463 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to solve the equation

$$
\sec x={\sqrt{2}}, \qquad  0^\circ\leq x <   360^\circ.
$$

Most calculators don't have a $\textrm{arcsec}{x}$ button, so we can't get a principal value immediately. However, by rewriting the equation in terms of $\cos{x}$, we can get a principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sec}x & =\sqrt{2} \\ \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}x} & =\sqrt{2} \\ \operatorname{cos}x & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can proceed as usual. Our principal value is

$$
x = \arccos \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right)= 45^\circ.
$$

Since $45^\circ$ lies inside the required domain, our first solution is $x_1=45^\circ.$ It lies in the first quadrant and has a reference angle $\theta_R = 45^\circ.$

Since $\cos{x} > 0,$ the second solution must lie in the fourth quadrant, and it also has a reference angle $\theta_R = 45^\circ.$

![](images/c7/c722d4fa2b77011e4df5b086c19bb09943446941484cfaf87559ca39a52183bc.png)

Since the second solution $x_2$ lies in the $4$th quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
x_2 = 360^\circ - 45^\circ = 315^\circ .
$$

So, the solutions are $x=45^\circ, 315^\circ.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "0fd2eba9-8794-5210-bea2-d726a0af4875" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2564 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "646dc860-2777-5e44-aa90-555d9b22ef5e" :step/math-academy-id 11842 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116025}} {:db/id 17592186116463 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to solve the equation

For example, suppose that we want to solve the equation

$$
\sec x = 2, \qquad -2\pi < x \leq 2\pi.
$$

We can proceed as usual. Recall that $\sec x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}.$ Therefore, the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\cos x = \dfrac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, we find the principal value:

$$
x = \arccos \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \right)= \dfrac{\pi}{3}
$$

Since $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ lies inside the required domain, our first solution is ${\color{red}x_1}=\dfrac{\pi}{3}.$ It is in the first quadrant and has a reference angle $\theta_R = \dfrac{\pi}{3}.$

Since $\cos{x} > 0,$ the second solution must lie in the fourth quadrant, and it also has a reference angle $\theta_R = \dfrac{\pi}{3}.$

![](images/31/318eba038feb091d6e3adb80ddf325de6039bb331a7713cf1e2c02171a6388d4.png)

Since the second solution $\color{blue}x_2$ lies in the $4$th quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
{\color{blue}x_2} = 2\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{5\pi}{3}
$$

However, we're not done yet. The domain $-2\pi < x \leq 2\pi$ is larger than one period, so there are more than two solutions.

To get the remaining solutions in the desired domain, we need to find angles that are coterminal with ${\color{red}x_1}$ or ${\color{blue}x_2}.$ So, we subtract integer multiples of $2\pi$ until all possible solutions are found:

$$
\eqalign{
x_3 & = {\color{red}x_1} -2\pi = \dfrac{\pi}{3}- 2\pi= -\dfrac{5\pi}{3},\
x_4 &= {\color{blue}x_2} -2\pi = \dfrac{5\pi}{3}- 2\pi= -\dfrac{\pi}{3}.}
$$

Adding or subtracting any more multiples of $2\pi$ would result in solutions outside the desired domain. So, we have found all the solutions.

Therefore, the solutions are  $x = \pm \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \pm \dfrac{5\pi}{3}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b5492203-ceec-581f-aede-beedabd8c432" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2565 :tutorial/title "Solving a Trigonometric Equation Involving Secant Under a Modified Domain"} :step/id #uuid "4e4240a5-e7ad-5cb0-a15b-ebc1ba39e102" :step/math-academy-id 11845 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116027}} {:db/id 17592186116464 :tutorial/content "We can solve an equation involving secant over any desired domain. - $A$ is the $3\times 3$ coefficient matrix,

- $\mathbf{x}$ is the column vector of variables, and

- $\mathbf{b}$ is the column vector of constants.

If the $3\times 3$ matrix $A$ is invertible, then we can find a solution to the system $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ by "pre-multiplying" both sides of the equation by $A^{-1}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}Ax & =b \\ {A}^{-1}Ax & ={A}^{-1}b \\ {I}_{3}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\ x & ={A}^{-1}b\end{aligned}
$$

So, to find the solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},$ we simply calculate $\mathbf{x}= A^{-1}\mathbf{b}.$

:question/math-academy-id "q-10091" :question/problem "Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}y+2z=0 \\ x+2y+3z=2 \\ 3x+y+z=-3\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =0|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|-1|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}|+2|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =0-1(1-9)+2(1-6) \\  & =+8-10 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -8 & -5 \\ -1 & -6 & -3 \\ -1 & -2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 8 & -5 \\ 1 & -6 & 3 \\ -1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 8 & -6 & 2 \\ -5 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 8 & -6 & 2 \\ -5 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -8 & 6 & -2 \\ 5 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -8 & 6 & -2 \\ 5 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{2} \\ 9 \\ -\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the solution is $x=-\frac{5}{2},y=9,z=-\frac{9}{2}.$"} :step/id #uuid "100a637e-a49a-5d4a-80d2-e88a9e19ca4c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186415693}} {:db/id 17592186415692 :step/content {:db/id 17592186348099 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6788781d-31d5-5bd7-b27b-68afaa4d9325" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=B\,d\,A" :db/id 17592186346254} {:answer/id #uuid "9bded5b5-b83d-570e-9629-cd29113e20b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=B\,d\,{A}^{-1}" :db/id 17592186346708} {:answer/id #uuid "a4a497d7-ea8a-5a5f-b4fd-1d8c483ff5a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x={A}^{-1}B\,d" :db/id 17592186346783} {:answer/id #uuid "b6d2cc68-86a2-5604-8401-931a07c9e6b8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=BA\,d" :db/id 17592186346945} {:answer/id #uuid "e304282a-e8e7-5d48-b8b7-fb2bbc3eab5d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=AB\,d" :db/id 17592186347347}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186347347} :answer-field/id #uuid "b4e01459-2873-55b9-8f7c-c4fb473002de" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186347921}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "5f0cd9e3-58c9-5ff5-838e-38f22a6e88cb" :question/math-academy-id "q-78570" :question/problem "Consider a matrix equation ${A}^{-1}\,x=B\,d,$ where $A$ and $B$ are $7\times 7$ non-singular matrices, while $x$ and $d$ are $7\times 1$ column vectors. for any real numbers $a$ and $b$ and any positive integer $n,$ 

$$
{(a + b)^n} = {n \choose 0}{a^n}{b^0} + {n \choose 1}{a^{n - 1}}{b^1} + {n \choose 2}{a^{n - 2}}{b^2} + \cdots + {n \choose n}{a^0}{b^n},
$$

where we recall that 

$$
{n \choose k} = \dfrac{n!}{k!\, (n-k)!  }.
$$

Let's use the binomial theorem to find the first few terms in the expansion of

$$
(2+x)^6.
$$

In this case, we have $a = 2,$ $b= x,$ and $n=6.$  Therefore, the first three terms of our expansion are given by

$$
{\left( {2 + x} \right)^{6}}   =  
{6\choose0}  {\left( 2 \right)^{6}}{\left( x \right)^0} +  {6\choose1}  {\left( 2 \right)^{6 - 1}}{\left( x \right)^1} +  {6\choose2}  {\left( 2 \right)^{6 - 2}}{\left( x \right)^2} + \cdots.
$$

Using a calculator, we find that

$$
{6\choose0} = {\color{blue}{1}}, \qquad {6\choose1} = {\color{blue}{6}}, \qquad {6\choose2} = {\color{blue}{15}}.
$$

Therefore, our expansion can be simplified as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(2+x)}^{6} & =(\frac{6}{0}){(2)}^{6}{(x)}^{0}+(\frac{6}{1}){(2)}^{6-1}{(x)}^{1}+(\frac{6}{2}){(2)}^{6-2}{(x)}^{2}+⋯ \\  & =(1)({2}^{6})(1)+(6)({2}^{5})(x)+(15)({2}^{4})({x}^{2})+⋯ \\  & =(1)(64)(1)+(6)(32)(x)+(15)(16)({x}^{2})+⋯ \\  & =64+192\,x+240\,{x}^{2}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "426cf476-6bfd-5054-aac9-8200164a34b5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3388 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "41da2623-7af5-5f79-be76-db13c7501f64" :step/math-academy-id 17592186106837 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107140 :tutorial/content "Recall that a random variable $X$ is a variable whose value is determined by the outcome of a trial or experiment. A random variable can take on one of many values from a set $S,$ called the range or support of $X.$

A **continuous random variable** is a random variable whose set of possible values $S$ is given by an interval of real numbers.

For example, the height of a randomly selected person could be modeled as a continuous random variable because its possible values form an interval of real numbers. For modeling purposes, we usually assume that the height of a randomly selected person could be *any number* in the real interval $(0,\infty),$ although we could also restrict this to a finite interval $[a,b]$ if we wanted.

On the other hand, the result of rolling a $6$-sided die is *not* a continuous random variable because its possible values are $1,2,3,4,5,6,$ which does *not* correspond to an interval of real numbers.

Physical quantities, such as mass, length, area, volume, time, fluid concentration, etc, are usually modeled as continuous variables. 

![](images/73/73d1a2c3852734a6221654882ad5421adb565c96c718e91283e5fbc1f26a72c7.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "56f14280-d510-530e-9f12-5e21e8dab7e7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6769 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "8a357dbd-8538-5f7a-a808-d0bb39634099" :step/math-academy-id 41069 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106838}} {:db/id 17592186106838 :step/content {:db/id 17592186105860 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105444 :question/id #uuid "e7c527c9-2dc1-50b2-bbf6-10c1a9d122dd" :question/math-academy-id "e-10837"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0ee39554-fd77-5e90-baa8-f9320ffc3398" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048368}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106529} {:db/id 17592186106531} {:db/id 17592186262582} {:db/id 17592186262583} {:db/id 17592186262584} {:db/id 17592186354550} {:db/id 17592186354551} {:db/id 17592186354552} {:db/id 17592186354553} {:db/id 17592186369331}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Continuous Random Variables Given in Context"} :step/id #uuid "6786cf48-e665-5cb3-ba1f-c245b903bc5f" :step/math-academy-id 41070 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106839}} {:db/id 17592186106839 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107141 :tutorial/content "The **probability density function** (or **pdf**) of a continuous random variable $X$ defined over a set $S$ is a function $f(x)$ such that the probability that $X$ lies in the interval $[a,b]$ is given by

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm dx.
$$

Thus, the probability that $X$ lies between $a$ and $b$ can be interpreted as the area bounded between $f(x)$ and the $x$-axis over the interval $x\in [a,b],$ as shown below.

![](images/e6/e6c21e69a0dbd15ce32d18c2e74d8fcab0276e82bc55b354eaa5140adff610e6.png)

In general, for a function $f(x)$ to be a valid probability density function over a set $S,$ it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x$ in $S$

- $\displaystyle \int_{S} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 1$

For example, let the random variable $X$ be the result of randomly selecting a real number between $0$ and $6.$ In this case, the pdf of $X$ is given by

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6},\, & 0\le x\le 6, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$

This pdf tells us that any number between $0$ and $6$ has an equal chance of being selected, and no number outside this interval can be selected. 

Note that this is a valid pdf because it's always nonnegative, and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{S}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{6}x]}_{0}^{6} \\  & =[\frac{1}{6}\cdot 6]-[\frac{1}{6}\cdot 0] \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the probability that our randomly selected number is no greater than $3,$ we integrate the pdf over the interval $[0,3]{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0\le X\le 3) & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{6}x]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =[\frac{1}{6}\cdot 3]-[\frac{1}{6}\cdot 0] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This result matches our intuition. Since every number has an equal chance of being selected, and $[0,3]$ is half the length of $[0,6],$ we must have $P(0 \leq X \leq 3) = \dfrac12.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "aeeb80c6-8faa-5653-8729-e6dc2c52a2e7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6770 :tutorial/title "Probability Density Functions"} :step/id #uuid "97ac3c7c-a2f7-585b-a8c6-99d14604c5d2" :step/math-academy-id 41073 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106840}} {:db/id 17592186106840 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107142 :tutorial/content "The probability density function of a continuous random variable $X$ is somewhat analogous to the probability *mass* function of a discrete random variable in the sense that it describes the probability distribution of $X.$ 

However, unlike the case with discrete random variables, probability density is *not* the same as probability! Instead, we can think of a pdf as a tool for computing probabilities for continuous random variables.  

There are two counterintuitive yet important points to be aware of when it comes to interpreting a pdf:

- *The probability that a continuous random variable takes on any particular value is always equal to $0.$* 

Continuing the previous example, the probability that our random variable takes on the value $X=5$ is equal to

$$
P(X = 5) = P(5 \leq X \leq 5) = \int_5^5 \dfrac{1}{6} \, \textrm dx = 0.
$$

In general, for any value $a$ and any continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x),$ we have

$$
P(X = a) = P(a \leq X \leq a) = \int_a^a f(x) \, \textrm dx = 0.
$$

- *The values of a probability density function may be greater than $1.$* 

For example, let $Y$ be the result of randomly selecting a real number between $0$ and $\dfrac{1}{2}.$ Then, the pdf of $Y$ is given by 

$$
f(y) = 2, \qquad y \in \left[ 0, \dfrac{1}{2} \right].
$$

This pdf tells us that all numbers between $0$ and $\dfrac{1}{2}$ are equally likely. Again, $f(y)$ is nonnegative, and 

$$
\int_0^{1/2} f(y) \, \textrm d y = \int_0^{1/2} 2 \, \textrm d y = 1.
$$

So, $f(y)$ is a valid probability density function.

Lastly, note that since the probability that a continuous random variable takes on a particular value is always equal to $0,$ it doesn't matter whether or not we include the endpoints of a particular interval. In other words, for any continuous random variable $X,$ we have

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = P(a < X < b) = P(a < X \leq b) = P(a \leq X < b) = \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm dx.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3bac600c-991c-55c0-8e73-72e609d149f5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6771 :tutorial/title "Interpreting Probability Density Functions"} :step/id #uuid :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186105985} {:db/id 17592186106837 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107140 :tutorial/content "Recall that a random variable $X$ is a variable whose value is determined by the outcome of a trial or experiment. A random variable can take on one of many values from a set $S,$ called the range or support of $X.$

A **continuous random variable** is a random variable whose set of possible values $S$ is given by an interval of real numbers.

For example, the height of a randomly selected person could be modeled as a continuous random variable because its possible values form an interval of real numbers. For modeling purposes, we usually assume that the height of a randomly selected person could be *any number* in the real interval $(0,\infty),$ although we could also restrict this to a finite interval $[a,b]$ if we wanted.

On the other hand, the result of rolling a $6$-sided die is *not* a continuous random variable because its possible values are $1,2,3,4,5,6,$ which does *not* correspond to an interval of real numbers.

Physical quantities, such as mass, length, area, volume, time, fluid concentration, etc, are usually modeled as continuous variables. 

![](images/73/73d1a2c3852734a6221654882ad5421adb565c96c718e91283e5fbc1f26a72c7.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "56f14280-d510-530e-9f12-5e21e8dab7e7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6769 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "8a357dbd-8538-5f7a-a808-d0bb39634099" :step/math-academy-id 41069 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106838}} {:db/id 17592186107140 :tutorial/content "Recall that a random variable $X$ is a variable whose value is determined by the outcome of a trial or experiment. On the other hand, the result of rolling a $6$-sided die is *not* a continuous random variable because its possible values are $1,2,3,4,5,6,$ which does *not* correspond to an interval of real numbers.

![](images/73/73d1a2c3852734a6221654882ad5421adb565c96c718e91283e5fbc1f26a72c7.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "56f14280-d510-530e-9f12-5e21e8dab7e7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6769 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186106838 :step/content {:db/id 17592186105860 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105444 :question/id #uuid "e7c527c9-2dc1-50b2-bbf6-10c1a9d122dd" :question/math-academy-id "e-10837"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0ee39554-fd77-5e90-baa8-f9320ffc3398" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048368}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106529} {:db/id 17592186106531} {:db/id 17592186262582} {:db/id 17592186262583} {:db/id 17592186262584} {:db/id 17592186354550} {:db/id 17592186354551} {:db/id 17592186354552} {:db/id 17592186354553} {:db/id 17592186369331}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Continuous Random Variables Given in Context"} :step/id #uuid "6786cf48-e665-5cb3-ba1f-c245b903bc5f" :step/math-academy-id 41070 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106839}} {:db/id 17592186106839 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107141 :tutorial/content "The **probability density function** (or **pdf**) of a continuous random variable $X$ defined over a set $S$ is a function $f(x)$ such that the probability that $X$ lies in the interval $[a,b]$ is given by

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm dx.
$$

Thus, the probability that $X$ lies between $a$ and $b$ can be interpreted as the area bounded between $f(x)$ and the $x$-axis over the interval $x\in [a,b],$ as shown below.

![](images/e6/e6c21e69a0dbd15ce32d18c2e74d8fcab0276e82bc55b354eaa5140adff610e6.png)

In general, for a function $f(x)$ to be a valid probability density function over a set $S,$ it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x$ in $S$

- $\displaystyle \int_{S} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 1$

For example, let the random variable $X$ be the result of randomly selecting a real number between $0$ and $6.$ In this case, the pdf of $X$ is given by

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6},\, & 0\le x\le 6, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$

This pdf tells us that any number between $0$ and $6$ has an equal chance of being selected, and no number outside this interval can be selected. 

Note that this is a valid pdf because it's always nonnegative, and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{S}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{6}x]}_{0}^{6} \\  & =[\frac{1}{6}\cdot 6]-[\frac{1}{6}\cdot 0] \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the probability that our randomly selected number is no greater than $3,$ we integrate the pdf over the interval $[0,3]{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0\le X\le 3) & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{6}x]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =[\frac{1}{6}\cdot 3]-[\frac{1}{6}\cdot 0] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This result matches our intuition. Since every number has an equal chance of being selected, and $[0,3]$ is half the length of $[0,6],$ we must have $P(0 \leq X \leq 3) = \dfrac12.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "aeeb80c6-8faa-5653-8729-e6dc2c52a2e7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6770 :tutorial/title "Probability Density Functions"} :step/id #uuid "97ac3c7c-a2f7-585b-a8c6-99d14604c5d2" :step/math-academy-id 41073 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106840}} {:db/id 17592186107141 :tutorial/content "The **probability density function** (or **pdf**) of a continuous random variable $X$ defined over a set $S$ is a function $f(x)$ such that the probability that $X$ lies in the interval $[a,b]$ is given by

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186093260 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093433 :tutorial/content "Consider the standard basis $\big\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \big\}$ of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the unit square spanned by these two vectors. 

Let's define a linear transformation $\mathbf R$ by its standard matrix $R,$ given by 

$$
[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}{30}^{∘} & -\operatorname{sin}{30}^{∘} \\ \operatorname{sin}{30}^{∘} & \operatorname{cos}{30}^{∘}\end{aligned}]
$$

We can find the images of $\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}$ under $\mathbf{R}$ by computing the matrix products, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{'} & =R(i)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}{30}^{∘} & -\operatorname{sin}{30}^{∘} \\ \operatorname{sin}{30}^{∘} & \operatorname{cos}{30}^{∘}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}{30}^{∘} \\ \operatorname{sin}{30}^{∘}\end{aligned}] \\ {j}^{'} & =R(j)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}{30}^{∘} & -\operatorname{sin}{30}^{∘} \\ \operatorname{sin}{30}^{∘} & \operatorname{cos}{30}^{∘}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}{30}^{∘} \\ \operatorname{cos}{30}^{∘}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Plotting the vectors $\mathbf i$ and $\mathbf j$ and their images $\mathbf i'$ and $\mathbf j',$ we obtain the following:

![](images/35/3516ba56a842adb78f1acae9190b65eb1574629e9f3d6bca25854f547f69385f.png)

We see that the transformation $\mathbf R$ represented by the matrix $R$ defines a **counterclockwise rotation of $30^\circ$ about the origin.**

As usual, we typically refer to rotations in the counterclockwise sense. However, in this case, the transformation $\mathbf R$ can also be considered a rotation of $360^\circ-30^\circ=330^\circ$ *clockwise* about the origin." :tutorial/id #uuid "427eca20-6aad-5c52-a545-fc66d808e5b6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3546 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "3b310d56-7a89-527c-bf59-b2f90684f0c7" :step/math-academy-id 464465 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093261}} {:db/id 17592186093261 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093435 :tutorial/content "The matrix $R_\theta,$ given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}\theta  & -\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}\theta  & \operatorname{cos}\theta \end{aligned}]
$$

represents a **rotation by an angle $\theta$ counterclockwise about the origin.**

To find the matrix representing a rotation by an angle $\theta$ *clockwise* about the origin, we replace $\theta$ with $-\theta$ in the above. This gives

$$
[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}(-\theta ) & -\operatorname{sin}(-\theta ) \\ \operatorname{sin}(-\theta ) & \operatorname{cos}(-\theta )\end{aligned}]
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "333a7749-1cde-5720-8a91-4a43d26fc0fd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3548 :tutorial/title "General Rotation Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "96b175ec-ed88-5e8d-8030-67a565348dd4" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186092431} {:db/id 17592186093260 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093433 :tutorial/content "Consider the standard basis $\big\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \big\}$ of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the unit square spanned by these two vectors. 

Let's define a linear transformation $\mathbf R$ by its standard matrix $R,$ given by 

$$
[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}{30}^{∘} & -\operatorname{sin}{30}^{∘} \\ \operatorname{sin}{30}^{∘} & \operatorname{cos}{30}^{∘}\end{aligned}]
$$

We can find the images of $\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}$ under $\mathbf{R}$ by computing the matrix products, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{'} & =R(i)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}{30}^{∘} & -\operatorname{sin}{30}^{∘} \\ \operatorname{sin}{30}^{∘} & \operatorname{cos}{30}^{∘}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}{30}^{∘} \\ \operatorname{sin}{30}^{∘}\end{aligned}] \\ {j}^{'} & =R(j)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}{30}^{∘} & -\operatorname{sin}{30}^{∘} \\ \operatorname{sin}{30}^{∘} & \operatorname{cos}{30}^{∘}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}{30}^{∘} \\ \operatorname{cos}{30}^{∘}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Plotting the vectors $\mathbf i$ and $\mathbf j$ and their images $\mathbf i'$ and $\mathbf j',$ we obtain the following:

![](images/35/3516ba56a842adb78f1acae9190b65eb1574629e9f3d6bca25854f547f69385f.png)

We see that the transformation $\mathbf R$ represented by the matrix $R$ defines a **counterclockwise rotation of $30^\circ$ about the origin.**

As usual, we typically refer to rotations in the counterclockwise sense. However, in this case, the transformation $\mathbf R$ can also be considered a rotation of $360^\circ-30^\circ=330^\circ$ *clockwise* about the origin." :tutorial/id #uuid "427eca20-6aad-5c52-a545-fc66d808e5b6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3546 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "3b310d56-7a89-527c-bf59-b2f90684f0c7" :step/math-academy-id 464465 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093261}} {:db/id 17592186093433 :tutorial/content "Consider the standard basis $\big\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \big\}$ of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the unit square spanned by these two vectors.

[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}\theta  & -\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}\theta  & \operatorname{cos}\theta \end{aligned}]

represents a **rotation by an angle $\theta$ counterclockwise about the origin.**

$$
[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}(-\theta ) & -\operatorname{sin}(-\theta ) \\ \operatorname{sin}(-\theta ) & \operatorname{cos}(-\theta )\end{aligned}]

For example, consider the following system and its associated augmented matrix:
![](images/1a/1ac826685473beeb7a7c0ee90465db019d0d5b70b1af562aa3469ae4f0a54007.svg)

To solve the system, we can reduce $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as usual. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & -6 & -10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -5 \\ 0 & 2 & -6 & -10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now
![](images/17/176e4c49ef19bb92d63190dc6674b66ee55b2fdb306293bae65b7f2b2935701d.svg)

Since any numbers $x,y,z$ form a solution of the final equation $0x+0y+0z = 0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of just two equations:

![](images/a9/a9dd77f0f2ac0f7bd04b5e70fdca3b126d4eb34b0c929caca48c60f138bc644d.svg)

The **basic variables** are the variables of our system whose coefficients are the pivots of the row echelon form matrix. Let's illustrate the pivots of $M\mathbin{:}$

![](images/1b/1b776faa6c69553ce04fbddc4e1aa45e18d7390a32ce34d9e0317b2fa83b8752.svg)

The pivots are

- $m_{11}=1,$ which is the coefficient of $x,$ and

- $m_{22}=1,$ which is the coefficient of $y.$

Therefore, the basic variables are $x$ and $y.$

The remaining variables are called the **free variables**. We have only one free variable in our system, which is $z$.

Finally, we can describe the **general solution** by finding equations for the basic variables in terms of the free variables. In our case, this means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z$.

To do this, we apply the back substitution. From the second equation, we obtain

$$
y - 3z = -5
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	y = -5+3z.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-(-5+3z)+z=2\,⟹\, & x=-3+2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is
![](images/e2/e21bb2b83534152d6bf3d1c43efbd301b42717b975f1f9ebaa28ee4bc3ef31bd.svg)
where $z$ (the free variable) is an arbitrary number.

In vector form, the solution can be written as
![](images/de/de7a613bbbde25e555608ebc419106701d47875e238832eab7533bf87b0f1ce8.svg)

Geometrically, this is the vector equation of a line, and any point on the line is a solution to our original system.

If we want to find some **particular solution** of the system, we simply choose some particular value of $z$ and find the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the line. For example, if we choose $z=0,$ then the corresponding values are $x=-3$ and $y=-5$ and the particular solution is $x=-3,$ $y=-5,$ $z=0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3f5fe61d-1298-5fad-8678-6cd961832dde" {:db/id 17592186050231 :topic/id #uuid "37ecf193-e06c-57b6-8b23-f7d295134db0" :topic/math-academy-id 1358} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186106667 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107088 :tutorial/content "Consider the standard basis $\big\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \big\}$ of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the unit square spanned by the vectors.

Let $[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$ be a matrix of a linear transformation $\mathbf T.$ We can find the images of $\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}$ under $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{'} & =T(i)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=2i \\ {j}^{'} & =T(j)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=j\end{aligned}
$$

Applying this transformation, we obtain the following image:

![](images/61/61fc1f3f1e76ff49b9967399d1b3a3a63bbe9845a59f2b2841af6e14510b2a7a.png)

We see that the transformation represented by the matrix $T$ multiplies the vector $\mathbf{i}$ by a factor of $2$ and leaves the vector $\mathbf j$ unchanged. This type of transformation is called a **stretch in the $\mathbf x$-direction.** We can also call it a **horizontal stretch.** In this case, we have a **horizontal stretch of scale factor** $\mathbf 2.$

In general, a stretch in the $x$-direction of scale factor $k$ with its center at the origin is represented by the matrix

$$
[\begin{aligned}k & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "2b251d5e-1184-5f44-b4ff-ba8c7a4fa35d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3538 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "24a98178-6804-578c-bcca-7be62c1fba55" :step/math-academy-id 20030 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106757}} {:db/id 17592186106668 :step/content {:db/id 17592186105764 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105616 :question/id #uuid "ffbe74ea-33e6-5998-8692-ed5d7bd0c30d" :question/math-academy-id "e-5450"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3105e8eb-010f-542b-9e40-12fda6ea00e7" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048203} {:db/id 17592186049020} {:db/id 17592186050136}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106489} {:db/id 17592186106490} {:db/id 17592186299626} {:db/id 17592186299627} {:db/id 17592186299628}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Standard Matrix of a Stretch Transformation Given a Vector and its Image"} :step/id #uuid "c1790453-592c-524b-85e4-b8f01da73075" :step/math-academy-id 20032 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106670}} {:db/id 17592186106669 :step/content {:db/id 17592186105765 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105617 :question/id #uuid "83ef303a-c25c-5cd5-8ab7-2c14cb05d433" :question/math-academy-id "e-5454"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "be42e4b3-4b15-589c-a7e1-23cc07083aff" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106305} {:db/id 17592186106306} {:db/id 17592186284561} {:db/id 17592186351290} {:db/id 17592186402588} {:db/id 17592186404170}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying a Shear or Stretch Transformation Given the Images of the Standard Basis Vectors"} :step/id #uuid "07af67d3-64da-5097-8283-afbf2a41a98e" :step/math-academy-id 20038 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106671}} {:db/id 17592186106670 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107089 :tutorial/content "Consider the standard basis $\big\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \big\}$ of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the unit square spanned by the vectors.

Let $[\begin{aligned}1 & 0.5 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$ be a matrix of a linear transformation $\mathbf T.$ We can find the images of $\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}$ under $\mathbf{T}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{'} & =T(i)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0.5 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=i \\ {j}^{'} & =T(j)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0.5 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=0.5i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Applying this transformation, we obtain the following image:

![](images/aa/aa646019f6af73e795661060a1a678b5b3be7961d7e60e3ae601d911033382d2.png)

The transformation represented by the matrix $T$ adds $0.5\mathbf{i}$ to $\mathbf j,$ while the vector $\mathbf i$ remains unchanged. This type of transformation is called a **horizontal shear.** In this case, we have a **horizontal shear with a shear factor of** $\mathbf{0.5}.$

In general, a horizontal shear of scale factor $k$ with its center at the origin is represented by the matrix

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & k \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]

$$

$$

$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f7ec9a33-b7de-5d47-a628-944e05516d52" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4415 :tutorial/title "Vertical Shear"} {:activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186097514} :activity/id #uuid "34909092-851c-5b8f-b289-94633fbc239b" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050267 :topic/id #uuid "3afe28a0-5051-52a1-a085-a06727c301b8" :topic/math-academy-id 1047} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186097514 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097840 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to solve the following system of linear equations:
![](images/b6/b6441688c486562e704a29317847ba53ca5130ff6e35c9d4effdea5ede005d3f.svg)
The augmented matrix for this system can be written as 
![](images/b4/b45896f12f8195fcb211411a9a2dcd230cee288822e2d37f2b364f6c1c831c6d.svg)

Notice that the matrix is in *row echelon form* (or REF). Whenever the augmented matrix is in row echelon form, we can solve the system using a method called **back substitution**.

Back substitution involves

- starting with the lowest equation (which is already solved for one variable),

- substituting the result into the next-lowest equation to find the solution for another variable, and

- continuing to substitute the result into the next-lowest equation until the values of all the variables have been found.

Here, the third equation states that $z=3.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
y -(3) = 2 
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	y = 5.
$$

Now, we substitute both $y=5$ and $z=3$ into the first equation to get

$$
x + 2(5) + (3) = 1
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	x = -12.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-12,$ $y=5,$ and $z=3.$ We can write it in vector form, as follows:

![](images/8b/8bbbabd0167fc73c58c095fb11ed5efb2c2dca63ee90e95717e26f30f0f170e9.svg)

**Note:** The values $x=-12,$ $y=5,$ and $z=3$ together form *one* solution. We say that this system has *one* solution, *not* three solutions. A system with three solutions would have three different solution vectors, whereas here, we only have *one* solution vector." :tutorial/id #uuid "4d84a9a0-94f9-57e2-a8e6-333ba26d72e4" :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186096855} {:db/id 17592186097514 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097840 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to solve the following system of linear equations:
![](images/b6/b6441688c486562e704a29317847ba53ca5130ff6e35c9d4effdea5ede005d3f.svg)
The augmented matrix for this system can be written as 
![](images/b4/b45896f12f8195fcb211411a9a2dcd230cee288822e2d37f2b364f6c1c831c6d.svg)

Notice that the matrix is in *row echelon form* (or REF). Whenever the augmented matrix is in row echelon form, we can solve the system using a method called **back substitution**.

Back substitution involves

- starting with the lowest equation (which is already solved for one variable),

- substituting the result into the next-lowest equation to find the solution for another variable, and

- continuing to substitute the result into the next-lowest equation until the values of all the variables have been found.

Here, the third equation states that $z=3.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
y -(3) = 2 
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	y = 5.
$$

Now, we substitute both $y=5$ and $z=3$ into the first equation to get

$$
x + 2(5) + (3) = 1
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	x = -12.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-12,$ $y=5,$ and $z=3.$ We can write it in vector form, as follows:

![](images/8b/8bbbabd0167fc73c58c095fb11ed5efb2c2dca63ee90e95717e26f30f0f170e9.svg)

**Note:** The values $x=-12,$ $y=5,$ and $z=3$ together form *one* solution. We say that this system has *one* solution, *not* three solutions. A system with three solutions would have three different solution vectors, whereas here, we only have *one* solution vector." :tutorial/id #uuid "4d84a9a0-94f9-57e2-a8e6-333ba26d72e4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3149 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "b94c8727-6dff-5c9a-9868-815a8a185978" :step/math-academy-id 17179 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097515}} {:db/id 17592186097840 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to solve the following system of linear equations:

17592186116106 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116490 :tutorial/content "Matrices can be used to represent systems of equations, such as the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2x+3y=5 \\ 4x\text{ }-\text{ }5y=-1\end{aligned}
$$

For a $2\times 2$ system like the one above, we put the coefficients of the system into a $2\times 2$ matrix, called the **coefficient matrix**:

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}]
$$

Each row has the coefficients of one of the equations in the system, and each column consists of the coefficients of one particular variable.
We also have the $2\times 1$ column vectors

$$
[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

where $\mathbf{b}$ consists of each constant on the right side of the system and $\mathbf{x}$ contains the variables.
With these matrices, we can write our system as $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b},$ or

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}]
$$

We can write any system of two equations with two variables in this form.
Just to check that the above equation is true, let's multiply out the left-hand side to see if it equals the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}Ax & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x+3y \\ 4x\text{ }-\text{ }5y\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =b\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "d49da49a-c3f8-5718-91a9-4adc236155d2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3048 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "f7a59c72-2c98-5267-942e-326053020128" :step/math-academy-id [{:db/id 17592186097476 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097831 :tutorial/content "It's often helpful to express a given vector in terms of sums and scalar multiples of a handful of known vectors.

As an example, let's consider the following diagram:

![](images/a6/a6c8dcdf9be32345bbc92ff162992e6c9cf02c107de8ff74caf534b508bfe411.png)

How can we express the vector $\overrightarrow{PR}$ in terms of the vectors $\textbf{a}$ and $\textbf{b}$ only?

According to the triangle law of addition,

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PR} & =\overset{\to }{PQ}+\overset{\to }{QR}\end{aligned}
$$

as shown below.

![](images/8c/8c72ba23124e9622b50f9daee4006ca4aac6a460b8a694a368d0e53393a85053.png)

From the original diagram, we have that

$$
{\color{blue}{\overrightarrow{PQ}}}   = \mathbf{a} \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
{\color{blue}{\overrightarrow{QR}}}  = -\mathbf{b}.
$$

![](images/9d/9d284b2d2683ae43fe57e8c96433803bc908d764e489ac0f861ad978393fde7d.png)

Therefore, by substituting these values into our equation for ${\color{red}\overrightarrow{PR}},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PR} & =\overset{\to }{PQ}+\overset{\to }{QR} \\  & =\text{a}+(-\text{b}) \\  & =\text{a}-\text{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's see another example." :tutorial/id #uuid "d92705a2-c9e5-5782-91e1-fa086fa5bffb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2904 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid 17592186096882} {:db/id 17592186097476 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097831 :tutorial/content "It's often helpful to express a given vector in terms of sums and scalar multiples of a handful of known vectors.

As an example, let's consider the following diagram:

![](images/a6/a6c8dcdf9be32345bbc92ff162992e6c9cf02c107de8ff74caf534b508bfe411.png)

How can we express the vector $\overrightarrow{PR}$ in terms of the vectors $\textbf{a}$ and $\textbf{b}$ only?

According to the triangle law of addition,

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PR} & =\overset{\to }{PQ}+\overset{\to }{QR}\end{aligned}
$$

as shown below.

![](images/8c/8c72ba23124e9622b50f9daee4006ca4aac6a460b8a694a368d0e53393a85053.png)

From the original diagram, we have that

$$
{\color{blue}{\overrightarrow{PQ}}}   = \mathbf{a} \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
{\color{blue}{\overrightarrow{QR}}}  = -\mathbf{b}.
$$

![](images/9d/9d284b2d2683ae43fe57e8c96433803bc908d764e489ac0f861ad978393fde7d.png)

Therefore, by substituting these values into our equation for ${\color{red}\overrightarrow{PR}},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PR} & =\overset{\to }{PQ}+\overset{\to }{QR} \\  & =\text{a}+(-\text{b}) \\  & =\text{a}-\text{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's see another example." :tutorial/id #uuid "d92705a2-c9e5-5782-91e1-fa086fa5bffb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2904 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "60458875-ac64-5849-86d5-1d54ffdf12af" :step/math-academy-id 15694 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097709}} {:db/id 17592186097831 :tutorial/content "It's often helpful to express a given vector in terms of sums and scalar multiples of a handful of known vectors.

:tutorial/content "Sometimes, we might have a system of equations with decimal coefficients, such as the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}0.2x+y=1 \\ 0.15x-0.04y=0.2\end{aligned}
$$

To make the system easier to solve, we turn it into a system involving integer coefficients only.

In general, we multiply each equation by $10,$ or $100,$ or $1000,$ etc. depending on how many decimal places we need to eliminate. In this particular instance:

- We need to eliminate one decimal place in the top equation, so we multiply by $10.$

- We need to eliminate two decimal places in the bottom equation, so we multiply by $100.$

So, we multiply the first equation by $10$ and the second equation by $100,$ as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}0.2x+y=1 & |\times 10 \\ 0.15x-0.04y=0.2 & |\times 100\end{aligned}
$$

From here, we can solve the system of equations using either substitution or elimination." :tutorial/id #uuid "ca705a2f-5d99-5642-87c9-9aadf1ef0319" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1465 :tutorial/title 17592186111822 :tutorial/content "Just as we can have a system of linear equations, we can also have systems of linear inequalities. For example, the system

![](images/42/422ff3fd1ff0704d34d5d2f098e3c524f409d2a4da7d6fa3d792020bbc8ac56d.svg)
is solved by the points that satisfy the inequalities ![](images/23/23f2bda2195f51e1cbf95f6905d547dc9004733d89866ae9f92ef046c330417c.svg) *and* ![](images/87/877dcbf886336f3054b3df8910cee950868e2819e007cf11544a6be7f15b81d3.svg) simultaneously.

To find the points that satisfy both inequalities, we first draw the graph of the inequality ![](images/9a/9a758452dbe8e0ede75fb97296110356c18e46275000ac28ebf631d91fa05b22.svg)

![](images/6f/6f3f7b6eb3109225256c5f4342333d03c19ef31b40d5ae5b24c136950a31f76a.png)

Now, on top of the diagram above, we draw the graph of the second inequality, ![](images/c1/c1e37a6573ce7b419aeff619c181b43325304505c05b669394ef0818ace2555f.svg)

![](images/e0/e017eefa235ac4b95009570c59fe5e5587f50bb02299305cfb9126573c0156bd.png)

The solution to the system is the *intersection* of the two regions (i.e., the part that is shaded twice).

![](images/c1/c1d9b4358e15ca09e8358f8e298fc0ffa745b885adcd7ea522e07f1d221a2c90.png)

The important thing to realize is that *any* point in the shaded region above satisfies *both* inequalities." :tutorial/id #uuid "1e005009-6033-5e6b-b50c-c802bbffe3e8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1473 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186111589 :step/content {:db/id 17592186110658 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110290 :question/id #uuid "4b19b389-7d0e-525b-b37f-787e53f5e3b2" :question/math-academy-id "e-1056"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0cd1bb61-2770-5096-83d6-d1e4a7189e9a" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048678} {:db/id 17592186050095}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186111052} {:db/id 17592186111235} {:db/id 17592186247068} {:db/id 17592186292531} {:db/id 17592186357444} {:db/id 17592186394827} {:db/id 17592186403037}] :knowledge-point/title "Working With Systems Containing "Or Equal To" Inequalities"} :step/id #uuid "712b9963-4a02-5cba-8c6c-337db89072ce" :step/math-academy-id 3483 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111579}} {:activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186116110} :activity/id #uuid "d07d2d5c-d3e0-595b-84ff-e18597a3d040" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050906 :topic/id #uuid "70425962-eba3-5483-950c-6e00e8bba0c0" :topic/math-academy-id 1730} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186116110 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116491 :tutorial/content "Consider a system of two linear equations with two variables

1045} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186097454 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097919 :tutorial/content "Sometimes, we might have a system of equations with fractional coefficients, such as the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{5}{4}y=-4 \\ 7x-5y=-2\end{aligned}
$$

We can turn the system into an equivalent system involving only integer coefficients. This will make it easier to solve.

In general, we multiply each equation by its lowest common denominator. In this instance, multiplying the first equation by the lowest common denominator of the fractions $(4)$ will do the job:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{5}{4}y=-4 & |\,\times 4 \\ 7x-5y=-2 & \end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve the system using, for example, the elimination method. Notice that the $5y$ term in the first equation can cancel with the $-5y$ term in the second equation.

Adding the two equations eliminates the $y$-variable, and allows us to solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+\cancel{5y} & =-16 \\ 7x-\cancel{5y} & =-2 \\ 9x & =-18 \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $x=-2$ into the equation $7x - 5y= -2$ to solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}7x-5y & =-2 \\ 7(-2)-5y & =-2 \\ -14-5y & =-2 \\ -5y & =12 \\ y & =-\frac{12}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=-2, \,y=-\dfrac{12}{5}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "68821d79-90e2-580a-95fd-a5268f848ff4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8706 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "703fc6f0-096a-5e00-b1a3-f32d4b4f9ac6" :step/math-academy-id 148710 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097455}} {:db/id 17592186097455 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096634 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096394 :question/id #uuid "fb7a4815-45e8-5288-8e96-c3741f1a2097" :question/math-academy-id "e-14732"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "14370371-529b-5f25-9963-62c0cd9a172e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049060}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186097189} {:db/id 17592186097319} {:db/id 17592186290328} {:db/id 17592186290329} {:db/id 17592186290330} {:db/id 17592186290335} {:db/id 17592186332888}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving a System Containing Fractions in One Equation Using Elimination"} :step/id #uuid "ef39da0c-015c-59a6-af08-1693a877674f" :step/math-academy-id 148711 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097456}} {:db/id 17592186097456 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096635 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096395 :question/id #uuid "7f77dc95-b22e-51af-a8c2-ef60ae4f3098" :question/math-academy-id "e-14733"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a7eb3fea-e4cf-5537-9a33-06b9d2b35c6b" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186097193} {:db/id 17592186097194} {:db/id 17592186290337} {:db/id 17592186290338} {:db/id 17592186332889} {:db/id 17592186345133}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving a System Containing Fractions in Both Equations Using Elimination"} :step/id #uuid "e0176cd1-6ae7-5332-9e2d-1cdfde89e84c" :step/math-academy-id 148714 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097457}} {:db/id 17592186097457 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097930 :tutorial/content "We can also use the substitution method to solve systems of equations containing fractional coefficients.

:step/content {:db/id 17592186097919 :tutorial/content "Sometimes, we might have a system of equations with fractional coefficients, such as the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{5}{4}y=-4 \\ 7x-5y=-2\end{aligned}
$$

We can turn the system into an equivalent system involving only integer coefficients. This will make it easier to solve.

In general, we multiply each equation by its lowest common denominator. In this instance, multiplying the first equation by the lowest common denominator of the fractions $(4)$ will do the job:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{5}{4}y=-4 & |\,\times 4 \\ 7x-5y=-2 & \end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve the system using, for example, the elimination method. Notice that the $5y$ term in the first equation can cancel with the $-5y$ term in the second equation.

Adding the two equations eliminates the $y$-variable, and allows us to solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+\cancel{5y} & =-16 \\ 7x-\cancel{5y} & =-2 \\ 9x & =-18 \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}7x-5y & =-2 \\ 7(-2)-5y & =-2 \\ -14-5y & =-2 \\ -5y & =12 \\ y & =-\frac{12}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=-2, \,y=-\dfrac{12}{5}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "68821d79-90e2-580a-95fd-a5268f848ff4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8706 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "703fc6f0-096a-5e00-b1a3-f32d4b4f9ac6" :step/math-academy-id 148710 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097455}} {:db/id 17592186097919 :tutorial/content "Sometimes, we might have a system of equations with fractional coefficients, such as the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{5}{4}y=-4 & |\,\times 4 \\ 7x-5y=-2 & \end{aligned}

Now, we can solve the system using, for example, the elimination method. Notice that the $5y$ term in the first equation can cancel with the $-5y$ term in the second equation.

$$

$$

Finally, we can substitute $x=-2$ into the equation $7x - 5y= -2$ to solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}7x-5y & =-2 \\ 7(-2)-5y & =-2 \\ -14-5y & =-2 \\ -5y & =12 \\ y & =-\frac{12}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}
$$

by "pre-multiplying" both sides of the equation by $A^{-1}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}Ax & =b \\ {A}^{-1}Ax & ={A}^{-1}b \\ {I}_{2}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\ x & ={A}^{-1}b\end{aligned}
$$

So, to find the solution of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b},$ we simply calculate $\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b}.$

For instance, to find the solution to the system of equations

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

 we first calculate the inverse of the coefficient matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$
This gives

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Then, the solution to this system is

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So the solution is $x=3$ and $y=2.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "39b17ee8-086a-5282-a414-c88d455b6107" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3049 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid system of equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}2x+y=3 \\ 6x+3y=9.\end{aligned}
$$

Can we use the matrix method of $\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ to find a solution to this system?

This system can be represented in the form $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ as

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

To use this matrix method, we need to find $A^{-1}.$ However

$$
\det (A) = 2\cdot 3 - 1\cdot 6 =0.
$$

Therefore, $A$ is not invertible. So we cannot use the matrix method to find a solution to the system.

In general, if the coefficient matrix $A$ is not invertible, there is no unique solution. This means that either

- a solution may not exist, or

- there may be infinitely many solutions." :tutorial/id #uuid "e5e2bff7-df5b-5628-92e3-a50ca8dd6be8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3066 :tutorial/title "Systems of Equations Where the Coefficient Matrix is Singular"} :step/id #uuid "ff58cfed-22a0-501b-8983-7edc00d85964" :step/math-academy-id 16614}] :activity/title "Solving 2x2 Systems of Equations Using Inverse Matrices" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186092433} {:db/id 17592186092992 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093402 :tutorial/content "If the $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ is invertible, then we can find a solution to the system

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = f(y),
$$

where the right-hand side doesn't depend explicitly on $x.$
We can classify each using the differential equation's phase line.

Let's see each type, and classify the equilibrium solutions for the differential equation whose phase line is shown below.

![](images/c6/c6fc21e9c83b98e055751ebd4062a3019687a885e2561191ec2d0bfd9de36a85.png)

- An equilibrium solution is a **sink** if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line both point *toward* the equilibrium solution.
For the phase line above, $y=2$ is a sink.

- An equilibrium solution is a **source** if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line both point *away* from the equilibrium solution. 
For the phase line above, $y=0$ is a source.

- An equilibrium solution is a **node** if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line point in the same direction.
For the phase line above, $y=-2$ is a node since the arrows above and below it both point downward." :tutorial/id #uuid "2f2f0bc9-a043-5c8e-92aa-88135e4033a9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5572 *autonomous* differential equation of the form

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = f(y),
$$

where the right-hand side doesn't depend explicitly on $x.$
We can classify each using the differential equation's phase line.

Let's see each type, and classify the equilibrium solutions for the differential equation whose phase line is shown below.

![](images/c6/c6fc21e9c83b98e055751ebd4062a3019687a885e2561191ec2d0bfd9de36a85.png)

- An equilibrium solution is a **sink** if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line both point *toward* the equilibrium solution.
For the phase line above, $y=2$ is a sink.

- An equilibrium solution is a **source** if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line both point *away* from the equilibrium solution. 
For the phase line above, $y=0$ is a source.

- An equilibrium solution is a **node** if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line point in the same direction.
For the phase line above, $y=-2$ is a node since the arrows above and below it both point downward." :tutorial/id #uuid "2f2f0bc9-a043-5c8e-92aa-88135e4033a9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5572 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "2e343aa9-f699-5b3e-a382-effdfef6dd15" :step/math-academy-id 594276 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148393}} {:db/id 17592186148771 :tutorial/content "There are three types of equilibrium solutions for an *autonomous* differential equation of the form

- An equilibrium solution is a *source* if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line both point *away* from the equilibrium solution.

- An equilibrium solution is a *node* if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line point in the same direction.

Therefore, we have:

- Statement I is false. From the phase line, we see that $y=2$ is a sink.

- Statement II is false, while statement III is true. From the phase line, we see that $y=-2$ is a source.

Note that there are $3$ equilibrium points, $y=-3,$ $y=0,$ and $y=3.$

- We're given that $y=-3$ is a sink. We represent this on the phase line by drawing a downward-pointing arrow just above $y=-3$ and an upward-pointing arrow just below it.

- We're given that $y=0$ is a source. We represent this on the phase line by drawing an upward-pointing arrow just above $y=-2$ and a downward-pointing arrow just below it (already drawn by the above property).

- We're given that $y=3$ is a sink. We represent this on the phase line by drawing a downward-pointing arrow just above $y=3$ and an upward-pointing arrow just below it (already drawn by the above property).

![](images/a4/a4d0e0f44f77e0d29d6d226b058806e947b38f4784dc61ea609ac1040b73d7dd.png)

Of the given options, the only slope field that correspond with this phase line is the following:

![](images/b5/b5e7a0272bb45b9d83ec8864f58cf3b96cbb6399d079f23d168d8de5416a1c23.png)

Note that:

- The slope field is horizontal at $y=-3,$ $y=0,$ and $y=3.$

- The slopes near $y=-3$ appear to converge toward this line.

- The slopes near $y=0$ appear to diverge away from this line.

- An equilibrium solution is a *sink* if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line both point *toward* the equilibrium solution.

- An equilibrium solution is a *source* if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line both point *away* from the equilibrium solution.

- An equilibrium solution is a *node* if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line point in the same direction.

First, we need to find the equilibrium solutions. So, we solve $f(y)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(y) & =0 \\ (y-3)({y}^{2}+3y+9) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equilibrium solution is $y=3.$ 

Now, we analyze the sign of $f(y)$ using a sign table, as follows:

|  | $(-\infty ,3)$ | $(3,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $y-3$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| ${y}^{2}+3y+9$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $f(y)$ | $-$ | $+$ |

So, we have that $f(y)$ is positive for $y\in (3,\infty ),$ and negative for $y\in (-\infty ,3).$

We can now draw the phase line for this equation.

![](images/24/244a46b17ad69e8d7cc3ae4f3d9c3c46c1d6e6a7ea154b849946f8ece6030071.png)

Finally, we classify the equilibrium solution:

- $y=3$ is a source because the nearby solutions diverge away from this point.

Which of the following could be the slope field of the differential equation?" :question/worked-solution "We can classify the equilibrium solutions of an autonomous ODE ${y}^{′}=f(y)$ by examining its phase line.

- An equilibrium solution is a *sink* if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line both point *toward* the equilibrium solution.

- An equilibrium solution is a *source* if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line both point *away* from the equilibrium solution.

- An equilibrium solution is a *node* if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line point in the same direction.

First, we draw the phase line with the given information. 

Note that there are $2$ equilibrium points, $y=0$ and $y=-4.$

- We're given that $y=0$ is a source. We represent this on the phase line by drawing an upward-pointing arrow just above $y=0$ and a downward-pointing arrow just below it.

- We're given that $y=-4$ is a sink. We represent this on the phase line by drawing a downward-pointing arrow just above $y=-4$ (already drawn by the above property) and an upward-pointing arrow just below it.

![](images/e5/e5ba765b9caffab904f07c5086d3206f72e36e66cb018673ce7ed44d79d19e88.png)

Of the given options, the only slope field that correspond with this phase line is the following:

![](images/41/41f32a097325dbe2a278da2abe4ef93b13d058ffe49431882fade3bc40bc0f48.png)

Note that:

- The slope field is horizontal at $y=0$ and $y=-4.$

- The slopes near $y=0$ appear to diverge away from this line.

- The slopes near $y=-4$ appear to converge toward this line."} :step/id #uuid "dc1c1dd6-77b7-596c-aadc-9bd547e58f0f" :step/next {:db/id 17592186414155}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid
