To see this, consider the set $\left\{ \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{0} \right\}.$ We can realize that this set is linearly dependent using either of the following two methods.

**Method 1**

Notice that 

$$
0 \cdot \mathbf{v} + 1 \cdot \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}.
$$

Therefore, the equation

$$
x_1 \mathbf{v} + x_2 \cdot \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}
$$

has a solution $x_1=0$ and $x_2=1,$ which is different from $x_1=x_2=0.$ So, the set is linearly dependent.

**Method 2**

Alternatively, recall that a set of two vectors is linearly dependent if and only if the two vectors are parallel. That is, the two vectors are multiples of each other.

The zero vector $\mathbf{0}$ is parallel to every other vector because it is a multiple of any other vector. For any vector $\mathbf{v},$ we have

$$
\mathbf{0} = 0 \cdot \mathbf{v} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \mathbf{0} \parallel \mathbf{v}.
$$

So, because $\mathbf{0}$ is parallel to $\mathbf{v},$ the set $\left\{ \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{0} \right\}$ is linearly dependent." :tutorial/id #uuid "ef2c96dd-d1cd-593e-a998-ba1be6c42686" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6812 :tutorial/title "Sets of Two Vectors Containing the Zero Vector"} :step/id #uuid "e814b4bf-688c-57df-8849-f4f2455723dd" :step/math-academy-id 41353 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120879}} {:db/id 17592186121123 :tutorial/content "Any set of two vectors that contains the zero vector $\mathbf{0}$ must be linearly dependent. However, these concepts can be extended to sets of any number of vectors.

A set of $n$ vectors $\left\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_n \right\}$ is called **linearly independent** if the only solution to the equation

$$
x_1 \mathbf{v}_1 + x_2 \mathbf{v}_2 + \ldots + x_n \mathbf{v}_n = \mathbf{0}
$$

is $x_1=x_2=\ldots=x_n=0.$ Otherwise, if there exists any solution other than $x_1 = x_2 = \ldots = x_n = 0,$ then we say that the set $\left\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_n \right\}$ is **linearly dependent**.

Similar to sets containing two vectors, a general set of $n$ vectors is dependent if *any* two vectors in the set are parallel.

**But be careful!** When working with sets containing more than two vectors, having a linearly dependent set is possible even if *none* of the vectors are parallel! 

For example, consider the following set of vectors: 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

None of the vectors in this set are parallel. However, we have

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the equation

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

has a solution $x_1 = 1,$ $x_2 = 1,$ and $x_3 = -1,$ which is different from $x_1 = x_2 = x_3 = 0.$ Therefore, we conclude that the vectors are linearly dependent." :tutorial/id #uuid "0d550a61-4219-5ffc-83a2-155ddd8fa9f4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6813 :tutorial/title "Linear Dependence and Independence for a General Set of Vectors"} :step/id #uuid "46556bbf-0804-5a49-af3c-3a10e60ee378" :step/math-academy-id 41357 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120881}} {:db/id 17592186121124 :tutorial/content "So far, we've discussed linear dependence and linear independence for sets of two vectors. {:db/id 17592186135022 :tutorial/content "The **intermediate value theorem (IVT)** states that:

> *If $f(x)$ is continuous on $\color{blue}[a,b],$ and $k$ is a number between $\color{red}{f(a)}$ and $\color{red}{f(b)}$ inclusively, then there exists a number $c \in \color{blue}{[a,b]}$ such that $f(c)=k.$*

The intuition behind the IVT is that if a function is continuous between two inputs, then between those two inputs, we must be able to draw the function without picking up our pen off the page, so the function must cover all values between the two corresponding outputs.

The IVT is often used to prove that some equation has a solution. For example, if we want to prove that there is a solution to $f(x)=3,$ and we know that $f(x)$ is a continuous function with $f({\color{blue}{1}})={\color{red}{2}}$ and $f({\color{blue}{6}})={\color{red}{6}},$ then the IVT tells us that there exists some solution $c \in \color{blue}{[1,6]}$ such that $f(c)=3.$

We can gain further intuition by visualizing the situation. First, let's plot what $y=f(x)$ *might* look like.

![](images/98/9896ea1c3d3d7c461e78ce4b4b232ce1f13f329468cd28b2d8e743132de093df.png)

For this particular $f(x)$ there is one solution to $f(x)=3$, which is $x\approx 2.$ Note that our solution lies inside the interval $\color{blue}[1,6].$

Now let's consider another *possible* $f(x).$

![](images/de/dea5683d5b18bccf9623fb6a107e8ef818ddd1cef4adbef08be471869791ec27.png)

This time, there are three solutions to $f(x)=3$ which lie in the interval $\color{blue}[1,6].$ 

We can keep changing our $f(x),$ but no matter how we draw it, we will always have some solution to $f(x)=3$ which lies in the interval $\color{blue}[1,6].$

![](images/4d/4d4aaec84baff10a48f715eeae7e06af21beccd29b38c42b3283032ef0726fec.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "9dc98e46-26fd-5ae1-b12b-05da48928cc5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 306 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "b8f1b0d3-494f-537b-8e99-af2aca4fc4f6" :step/math-academy-id 564 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134752}} {:db/id 17592186134976 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133955 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133477 :question/id #uuid "bb373a5d-aa71-58ed-82e3-b74a8f51d144" :question/math-academy-id "e-114"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6388d315-340b-56a0-bc93-e380bfbf6ed3" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134471} {:db/id 17592186134474} {:db/id 17592186241105} {:db/id 17592186348086} {:db/id 17592186397801} {:db/id 17592186398841}] :knowledge-point/title "Selecting a Specific Value For Which a Solution Is Guaranteed"} :step/id #uuid "ce1aa6a3-c0f2-525f-a909-c241964d206f" :step/math-academy-id 565 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134977}} {:db/id 17592186134977 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133956 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133478 :question/id #uuid "d048aae2-5773-5da7-ab18-35d41bfbb53a" :question/math-academy-id "e-115"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7dffa987-022c-52a2-bc21-cdace7455eab" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134470} {:db/id 17592186134516} {:db/id 17592186317540} {:db/id 17592186329804} {:db/id 17592186348091} {:db/id 17592186348092} {:db/id 17592186399489}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining the Number of Solutions Given a Table of Values of a Continuous Function"} :step/id #uuid "804af12a-0f60-55f9-a36a-0d40e8fd270b" :step/math-academy-id 568 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134978}} {:db/id 17592186134978 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135023 :tutorial/content "Consider the function $f(x)$ given below.

$$
{\begin{aligned}-x+5, & 1\le x<3 \\ -x+4, & 3\le x<4\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Can we apply the intermediate value theorem to $f(x)$ on the interval $[1,4]?$

Remember, the intermediate value theorem assumes that the function is continuous. Here, the function $f(x)$ not continuous on $[1,4].$ So, we cannot apply the intermediate value theorem.

If we plot the function, we can get an idea of why the intermediate value theorem cannot be applied.

![](images/9b/9b9543ec11b350cea4ca18e24a8db6ae8f72ffc38e64f973f9af2f83f1226400.png)

The graph shows that, for example, the equation $f(x)=1.5$ has no solution on $[1,4]$ despite the fact that $1.5$ lies between $f(1)=4$ and $f(4)=0.$
So, the intermediate value theorem does not hold.

**Watch out!** The interval on which we apply the intermediate value theorem must *always* be closed. > *If $f(x)$ is continuous on $\color{blue}[a,b],$ and $k$ is a number between $\color{red}{f(a)}$ and $\color{red}{f(b)}$ inclusively, then there exists a number $c \in \color{blue}{[a,b]}$ such that $f(c)=k.$*

The intuition behind the IVT is that if a function is continuous between two inputs, then between those two inputs, we must be able to draw the function without picking up our pen off the page, so the function must cover all values between the two corresponding outputs.

The IVT is often used to prove that some equation has a solution. For example, if we want to prove that there is a solution to $f(x)=3,$ and we know that $f(x)$ is a continuous function with $f({\color{blue}{1}})={\color{red}{2}}$ and $f({\color{blue}{6}})={\color{red}{6}},$ then the IVT tells us that there exists some solution $c \in \color{blue}{[1,6]}$ such that $f(c)=3.$

We can gain further intuition by visualizing the situation. First, let's plot what $y=f(x)$ *might* look like.

![](images/98/9896ea1c3d3d7c461e78ce4b4b232ce1f13f329468cd28b2d8e743132de093df.png)

For this particular $f(x)$ there is one solution to $f(x)=3$, which is $x\approx 2.$ Note that our solution lies inside the interval $\color{blue}[1,6].$

Now let's consider another *possible* $f(x).$

![](images/de/dea5683d5b18bccf9623fb6a107e8ef818ddd1cef4adbef08be471869791ec27.png)

This time, there are three solutions to $f(x)=3$ which lie in the interval $\color{blue}[1,6].$ 

We can keep changing our $f(x),$ but no matter how we draw it, we will always have some solution to $f(x)=3$ which lies in the interval $\color{blue}[1,6].$

$$
{\begin{aligned}-x+5, & 1\le x<3 \\ -x+4, & 3\le x<4\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Can we apply the intermediate value theorem to $f(x)$ on the interval $[1,4]?$

Remember, the intermediate value theorem assumes that the function is continuous. Here, the function $f(x)$ not continuous on $[1,4].$ So, we cannot apply the intermediate value theorem.

If we plot the function, we can get an idea of why the intermediate value theorem cannot be applied.

![](images/9b/9b9543ec11b350cea4ca18e24a8db6ae8f72ffc38e64f973f9af2f83f1226400.png)

The graph shows that, for example, the equation $f(x)=1.5$ has no solution on $[1,4]$ despite the fact that $1.5$ lies between $f(1)=4$ and $f(4)=0.$
So, the intermediate value theorem does not hold.

**Watch out!** The interval on which we apply the intermediate value theorem must *always* be closed. First, we note that the position vector of the point $P$ is $\mathbf{p}=\langle -7,5,-2 \rangle,$ and we can write down the equation of the plane using the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨3,-6,5⟩ & =⟨-7,5,-2⟩\cdot ⟨3,-6,5⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨3,-6,5⟩ & =-61\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to obtain the Cartesian equation, we substitute $\mathbf{r}=\langle x,y,z \rangle$ into the equation above and get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨3,-6,5⟩ & =-61 \\ 3x-6y+5z & =-61 \\ 3x-6y+5z+61 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This final equation is called the **Cartesian equation of the plane**.

![](images/77/77f18981dda500889655225eabbec730b7b295e6b16cec1700d56c2e27e0ac91.png)

Note that in the equation 

$$
{\color{blue}3}x+({\color{blue}-6})y+{\color{blue}5}z+61 = 0,
$$

the coefficients next to $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ are the coordinates of the normal vector 

$$
\mathbf{n}=\langle {\color{blue}3},{\color{blue}-6},{\color{blue}5} \rangle
$$

." :tutorial/id #uuid "81332607-6152-5770-b33d-8b80c630fc8d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3256 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c247ca81-f4a5-53d1-8429-f69593877343" :step/math-academy-id :question/math-academy-id "q-70807" :question/problem "Find a Cartesian equation of the plane that passes through the point $P(1,-1,1)$ and is perpendicular to the line 
$\frac{x-2}{-1}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z+1}{1}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that the position vector of $P$ is $p=⟨1,-1,1⟩.$ From the canonical equation, we find that the line is parallel to the vector $⟨-1,2,1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of the plane is 

$$
n=⟨-1,2,1⟩.
$$

Using the dot product, we can find the equation of the plane as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨-1,2,1⟩ & =⟨1,-1,1⟩\cdot ⟨-1,2,1⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨-1,2,1⟩ & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to obtain the Cartesian equation of the plane, we substitute $r=⟨x,y,z⟩$ into the equation above and get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨-1,2,1⟩ & =-2 \\ -x+2y+z & =-2 \\ -x+2y+z+2 & =0 \\ x-2y-z-2 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "4426cd88-0ed0-5a8a-bd40-151d1e9d59dd" :step/next {:db/id 17592186419428}} {:db/id 17592186419425 :step/content {:db/id 17592186419421 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "66b70f6a-e851-54e5-aa28-b6a025e9ece5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "57" :db/id 17592186419408}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186419408} :answer-field/id #uuid "2f1bb041-bd3b-51ec-95b9-ab27a720aff3" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186419416} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b0061273-aae7-5a50-ba3b-7dbc44ba608c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186419411}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186419411} :answer-field/id #uuid "51f6537d-feab-5ce3-9fc6-f89624d037a2" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186419418} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "373d6628-e7af-5c99-8ea7-bda3f45e1294" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186419407}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186419407} :answer-field/id #uuid "c79424ce-ee00-57d0-b195-b7db6dde7351" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186419420}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "53aad395-ec2e-5a47-9cdb-e404625e4482" :question/math-academy-id "q-330576" :question/problem "Find a Cartesian equation of the plane that passes through the point $P(7,4,-3)$ and is perpendicular to the line 
$\frac{x-3}{5}=\frac{y-2}{4}=\frac{z+1}{-2}.$

{{field-1}}
$x\,+4y\,-$
{{field-2}}
$z\,-$
{{field-3}}
$=0$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that the position vector of $P$ is $p=⟨7,4,-3⟩.$ From the canonical equation, we find that the line is parallel to the vector $⟨5,4,-2⟩.$ So, the normal vector of the plane is 

$$
n=⟨5,4,-2⟩.
$$

Using the dot product, we can find the equation of the plane as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨5,4,-2⟩ & =⟨7,4,-3⟩\cdot ⟨5,4,-2⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨5,4,-2⟩ & =57\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to obtain the Cartesian equation of the plane, we substitute $r=⟨x,y,z⟩$ into the equation above and get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨5,4,-2⟩ & =57 \\ 5x+4y-2z & =57 \\ 5x+4y-2z-57 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "62621dfb-b37e-5d44-bdc0-8c2aa74e902d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186419426}} {:db/id 17592186419426 :step/content {:db/id 17592186311671 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "43ac71e4-1f43-51f8-bfa4-a92855f4700b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-6" :db/id 17592186309261}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186309261} :answer-field/id #uuid "7faaceec-cd8b-568a-858c-271760090279" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186311144} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "580b7964-a0b4-59ea-bd21-b56d80484ba8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186309413}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186309413} :answer-field/id #uuid "93f3390e-533a-5d25-83c0-c5daa77f3ccf" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186311213} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0ccc2dae-6d3d-5c97-a2ff-2660720cb731" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5" :db/id 17592186308836}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186308836} :answer-field/id #uuid "95d0ab30-64b1-59c5-b1be-e3cbd8256de2" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186311226}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "04886b81-54da-502a-b95c-1502eb418ce2" :question/math-academy-id "q-336241" :question/problem "Given the Cartesian equation $12y-6z-30=0$ of the plane $Π$, find an equation of $Π$ in the form $(r-p)\cdot n=0.$

$(r-⟨0,0,$
{{field-1}}

{{field-2}}

$⟩=0$" :question/worked-solution "First, from the equation of the plane we get that the normal vector of $Π$ is $n=⟨0,12,-6⟩.$

Now, we solve the Cartesian equation of $Π$ for $z$:

$$
\begin{aligned}12y-6z-30 & =0 \\ -6z & =-12y+30 \\ z & =2y-5\end{aligned}
$$

If we put, say, $y=0$, we get $z=-5.$ Hence, the point $P(0,0,-5)$ lies on $Π.$ Note that the position vector of $P$ is $p=⟨0,0,-5⟩.$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ (r-⟨0,0,-5⟩)\cdot ⟨0,12,-6⟩ & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6908c1c1-4988-5f64-8e7b-f1732fcb1a7f"} {:db/id 17592186419427 :step/content {:db/id 17592186419423 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "102de1fa-9039-5418-a721-6fc419237fc4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+5y+8z+9=0" :db/id 17592186419404} {:answer/id #uuid "90536ec6-2590-5af2-a702-9be2e4b1ecdc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+8y+5z+6=0" :db/id 17592186419409} {:answer/id #uuid "c7f81252-3be5-5daa-a718-63070020d187" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-5y+8z+7=0" :db/id 17592186419413} {:answer/id #uuid "c8ca9437-ca61-5c50-96e0-f167dfcd51fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+5y-8z+11=0" :db/id 17592186419414} {:answer/id #uuid "d6eccb3f-c3a2-58a8-b47e-683c853ab3af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+5y+9z+15=0" :db/id 17592186419415}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186419404} :answer-field/id #uuid "34e50549-8287-5dd0-82ee-b77b6017695a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186419417}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "e08b1f6c-36a3-5d41-8737-49d26e8563c5" :question/math-academy-id "q-128459" :question/problem "Find a Cartesian equation of the plane that passes through the points $A(1,-2,0)$, $P(3,-4,1)$ and $Q(2,1,-2).$" :question/worked-solution "Note that the position vectors of the points $A,P$ and $Q$ are $a=⟨1,-2,0⟩,\,p=⟨3,-4,1⟩,$ and $q=⟨2,1,-2⟩.$

First, using the $3$ points we build $2$ vectors parallel to the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} & =\overset{\to }{AP} \\  & =⟨3,-4,1⟩-⟨1,-2,0⟩ \\  & =⟨2,-2,1⟩ \\ {v}_{2} & =\overset{\to }{AQ} \\  & =⟨2,1,-2⟩-⟨1,-2,0⟩ \\  & =⟨1,3,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find the normal vector of the plane. To do that, we use the cross product of ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}n & ={v}_{1}\times {v}_{2} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\times [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & -2\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =i+5j+8k \\  & =⟨1,5,8⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the dot product, we can find the equation of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨1,5,8⟩ & =⟨3,-4,1⟩\cdot ⟨1,5,8⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨1,5,8⟩ & =-9\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to obtain the Cartesian equation of the plane, we substitute $r=⟨x,y,z⟩$ into the equation above and get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨1,5,8⟩ & =-9 \\ x+5y+8z & =-9 \\ x+5y+8z+9 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6d308039-35f2-59e5-b262-324c1a8c2bf2" :step/next {:db/id 17592186419425}} {:db/id 17592186419428 :step/content {:db/id 17592186262889 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0f87268c-9742-5090-b7cb-521a5d8bbe66" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(r-⟨0,0,1⟩)\cdot ⟨2,4,-4⟩=0" :db/id 17592186260021} {:answer/id #uuid "a390ff13-0937-5eb3-b38b-3df5883b8889" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(r-⟨0,0,-2⟩)\cdot ⟨-4,4,-2⟩=0" :db/id 17592186261300} {:answer/id #uuid "def43d7d-583f-5acb-a4e0-a37562571a5c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(r-⟨0,0,0⟩)\cdot ⟨4,-2,4⟩=0" :db/id 17592186261844} {:answer/id #uuid "f4c13bd5-c05b-5f70-93b5-0ba177da222f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(r-⟨0,0,0⟩)\cdot ⟨4,4,-2⟩=0" :db/id 17592186262013} {:answer/id #uuid "ffcc7a65-376c-57d0-ac3e-a501019e18ce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(r-⟨0,0,2⟩)\cdot ⟨4,4,2⟩=0" :db/id 17592186262119}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186262013} :answer-field/id #uuid "7b80e560-2ad7-58b7-9b2c-28eb67acbc7c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186262329}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0f6aca53-4308-58bc-afcc-f2738d69d1e0" :question/math-academy-id "q-128380" :question/problem "Given the Cartesian equation $4x+4y-2z=0$ of the plane $Π$, find an equation of $Π$ in the form $(r-p)\cdot n=0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, from the equation of the plane we get that the normal vector of $Π$ is $n=⟨4,4,-2⟩.$

Now, we solve the Cartesian equation of $Π$ for $z$:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+4y-2z & =0 \\ 2z & =4x+4y \\ z & =2x+2y.\end{aligned}
$$

If we put, say, $x=0$ and $y=0$, we get $z=0.$ Hence, the point $P(0,0,0)$ lies on $Π.$ Note that the position vector of $P$ is $p=⟨0,0,0⟩.$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ (r-⟨0,0,0⟩)\cdot ⟨4,4,-2⟩ & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c018d688-d281-50de-9674-51b7847b124c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186419427}}] :activity/title "The Cartesian Equation of a Plane" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186419402} {:db/id 17592186419424 :step/content {:db/id 17592186419422 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "08c0fd5d-eb30-51ed-9d57-ff0d86d1b905" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-y+z-2=0" :db/id 17592186419403} {:answer/id #uuid "25dcf144-1a51-5366-9800-5383c00b5a7d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-2y-z-2=0" :db/id 17592186419405} {:answer/id #uuid "2b822cf8-78b8-5c6f-ba5e-a61ce1027e3a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-2y-z-5=0" :db/id 17592186419406} {:answer/id #uuid "aaf4ea99-1c7e-5b6b-af27-f81db06966e0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-x-2y-z-5=0" :db/id 17592186419410} {:answer/id #uuid "b32a3885-cdf4-51dc-ad0e-0a3c46647043" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-y+z-5=0" :db/id 17592186419412}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186419405} :answer-field/id #uuid "b30e511f-0a3e-547f-96f1-0bfc53ad4766" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186419419}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "70aeaa22-2b90-533e-ab1d-9dbd9f885f48" :question/math-academy-id "q-70807" :question/problem "Find a Cartesian equation of the plane that passes through the point $P(1,-1,1)$ and is perpendicular to the line

:question/math-academy-id "q-128459" :question/problem "Find a Cartesian equation of the plane that passes through the points $A(1,-2,0)$, $P(3,-4,1)$ and $Q(2,1,-2).$" :question/worked-solution "Note that the position vectors of the points $A,P$ and $Q$ are $a=⟨1,-2,0⟩,\,p=⟨3,-4,1⟩,$ and $q=⟨2,1,-2⟩.$

First, using the $3$ points we build $2$ vectors parallel to the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} & =\overset{\to }{AP} \\  & =⟨3,-4,1⟩-⟨1,-2,0⟩ \\  & =⟨2,-2,1⟩ \\ {v}_{2} & =\overset{\to }{AQ} \\  & =⟨2,1,-2⟩-⟨1,-2,0⟩ \\  & =⟨1,3,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find the normal vector of the plane. To do that, we use the cross product of ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}n & ={v}_{1}\times {v}_{2} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\times [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & -2\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =i+5j+8k \\  & =⟨1,5,8⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the dot product, we can find the equation of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨1,5,8⟩ & =⟨3,-4,1⟩\cdot ⟨1,5,8⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨1,5,8⟩ & =-9\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to obtain the Cartesian equation of the plane, we substitute $r=⟨x,y,z⟩$ into the equation above and get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨1,5,8⟩ & =-9 \\ x+5y+8z & =-9 \\ x+5y+8z+9 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6d308039-35f2-59e5-b262-324c1a8c2bf2" :step/next {:db/id 17592186419425}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "102de1fa-9039-5418-a721-6fc419237fc4" :answer/type {:db/id :step/next {:db/id 17592186148281}} {:db/id 17592186148280 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148744 :tutorial/content "In general, given two planes

- *Case 3*:  If the corresponding coefficients of ${\Pi_{{1}}}$ and ${\Pi_{{2}}}$ are all proportional, then the planes are coincident." :tutorial/id #uuid "50ffbdb5-c9d0-5815-9b29-b505cde7f0fa" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3804 :tutorial/title "Intersection of Two Planes in 3D"} :step/id #uuid "cba5c95d-7e83-5872-ae95-b6832ff486a2" :step/math-academy-id 21955 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148279}} {:db/id 17592186148281 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148745 :tutorial/content "Consider a line that is given by its vector equation

I. The cross product of the normal vectors of the planes is equal to $⟨1,1,0⟩.$

II. The planes intersect on a line.

III. The planes are coincident." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that:

- For the plane $x+y+z=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,1,1⟩.$

- For the plane $x+y+1=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,1,0⟩.$

Now, let's consider the statements.

- Statement I is false. Indeed, computing the cross product of the normal vectors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,1,1⟩\times ⟨1,1,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i+j \\  & =⟨-1,1,0⟩\ne ⟨1,1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Since ${n}_{1}\times {n}_{2}\ne 0$, the vectors ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are not parallel. Hence, the corresponding planes must intersect on a line.

17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "caefbcdd-6450-5b4b-b965-772f5b87b02a" :question/math-academy-id "q-129208" :question/problem "The intersection of the planes $2x+3y-3=0$ and $3x+z+19=0$ is given by the line

$$
r(t)=⟨0,{a}_{2},{a}_{3}⟩+tb,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Calculate ${a}_{2}-{a}_{3},$ and find a possible direction vector $b.$" :question/worked-solution "We're given that there exists a point on the line where $x=0.$ Substituting this to the first equation gives

$$
0+3y-3=0\,⟹\,y=1,
$$

and substituting $x=0$ into the second equation gives

$$
0+z+19=0\,⟹\,z=-19.
$$

Therefore, $a=⟨0,1,-19⟩$ is a position vector of a point on the line.

Next, we notice:

- For the plane $2x+3y-3=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨2,3,0⟩.$

- For the plane $3x+z+19=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨3,0,1⟩.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}b & ={n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} \\  & =⟨2,3,0⟩\times ⟨3,0,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =3i-2j-9k \\  & =⟨3,-2,-9⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The equation of the line is:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+tb \\ r(t) & =⟨0,1,-19⟩+t⟨3,-2,-9⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then, ${a}_{2}-{a}_{3}=1-(-19)=20,$ and $b=⟨3,-2,-9⟩.$"} :step/id #uuid "c6d8b30b-6627-55c2-a300-1bd06da939e9" :step/next {:db/id 17592186421904}} {:db/id 17592186421904 :step/content {:db/id 17592186262998 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2bbb0f75-5837-5fef-9156-1bb0626a6799" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}=-3,\,b=⟨-1,1,2⟩" :db/id 17592186260264} {:answer/id #uuid "358aeb92-2af7-5b63-a3fc-98a16739711a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}=6,\,b=⟨-2,1,1⟩" :db/id 17592186260355} {:answer/id #uuid "4ae1bb4f-6418-5cbe-8748-f187b44dbec8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}=3,\,b=⟨-1,2,1⟩" :db/id 17592186260517} {:answer/id #uuid "83b18a92-b695-5c83-b721-b2dee329f376" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}=-6,\,b=⟨-2,1,-1⟩" :db/id 17592186261019} {:answer/id #uuid "db99d772-027a-5c17-b647-51f20577ed39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}=5,\,b=⟨1,2,1⟩" :db/id 17592186261817}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186260517} :answer-field/id #uuid "3e5261fb-a30e-5c21-b272-d448a6432184" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186262235}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ad00dc96-c374-5320-be1d-ca73d7e96f79" :question/math-academy-id "q-129238" :question/problem "The intersection of the planes $x+y-z-3=0$ and $x+2y-3z+18=0$ is given by the line

$$

$$

Calculate ${a}_{1}+{a}_{2},$ and find a possible direction vector $b.$" :question/worked-solution "We're given that there exists a point on the line where $z=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation gives  

$$
x+y-0-3=0\,⟹\,x=3-y,
$$

and substituting $z=0$ and $x=3-y$ into the second equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(3-y)+2y-3(0)+18 & =0 \\ 3+y+18 & =0 \\ y & =-21.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=3-y=3+21=24$ and $a=⟨24,-21,0⟩$ is a position vector of a point on the line.

Next, we notice:

- For the plane $x+y-z-3=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,1,-1⟩.$

- For the plane $x+2y-3z+18=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,2,-3⟩.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,1,-1⟩\times ⟨1,2,-3⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i+2j+k \\  & =⟨-1,2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the equation of the line is:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+tb \\ r(t) & =⟨24,-21,0⟩+t⟨-1,2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then, ${a}_{1}+{a}_{2}=24-21=3,$ and $b=⟨-1,2,1⟩.$"} :step/id #uuid "4b62f78b-d432-5341-a2aa-4388a4c716e4"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2bbb0f75-5837-5fef-9156-1bb0626a6799" "Given the two planes $3x+3y+2z=0$ and $x-y-z=0$, which of the following statements are true?

I. The cross product of the normal vectors of the planes is equal to $⟨1,6,-5⟩.$

II. The planes are parallel.

III. The planes intersect on a line." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that:

- For the plane $3x+3y+2z=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨3,3,2⟩.$

- For the plane $x-y-z=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,-1,-1⟩.$

Now, let's consider the statements.

- Statement I is false. Computing the cross product of the normal vectors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨3,3,2⟩\times ⟨1,-1,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 3 & 3 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i+5j-6k \\  & =⟨-1,5,-6⟩\ne ⟨1,6,-5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Since ${n}_{1}\times {n}_{2}\ne 0$, the vectors ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are not parallel. As a result, the corresponding planes are not parallel either.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, two non-parallel planes in $3$-dimensional space must intersect on a line.

Therefore, only statement III is true."} :step/id #uuid "8993a320-0fa1-5bea-8343-47ddcfb4405b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186421903}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid [{:db/id 17592186162952 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163262 :tutorial/content "We often want to know if there is a relationship between two random variables. For this reason, we wish to formulate the idea of a joint probability distribution.

To introduce this concept, suppose the random variable $X$ represents the number of heads obtained when a fair coin is flipped. The support of $X,$ denoted $S_X,$ consists of all possible values of $X$ and in this case is given by

$$
S_X = \{0,1\}.
$$

Now suppose that the random variable $Y$ represents the result of rolling a fair tetrahedral die. Then the support of $Y,$ denoted $S_Y,$ is

$$
S_Y = \{1,2,3,4\}.
$$

The **joint support** of $X$ and $Y,$ denoted $S,$ consists of all possible pairs $(x,y)$ such that $x$ is a possible outcome for $X$ and $y$ is a possible outcome for $Y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(0,1), & (0,2), & (0,3), & (0,4) \\ (1,1), & (1,2), & (1,3), & (1,4)\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $S_X\times S_Y$ is the cartesian product of $S_X$ and $S_Y.$

A **joint probability distribution** is a probability distribution over a set of pairs [math](X, Y),[/math] where [math]X[/math] and [math]Y[/math] are both random variables. In this lesson, we will focus on the case where [math]X[/math] and [math]Y[/math] are *discrete* random variables, in which case the joint probability distribution is called a **joint probability mass function**. 

Let's assume that the flipping of the coin and rolling of the die are independent. Then, for any $x \in X$ and any $y \in Y,$ we have that

$$
P(X=x\:\textrm{and}\:Y=y) = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1}{8}.
$$

 

The **joint probability mass function** of $X$ and $Y,$ denoted $f(x,y),$ can be represented by the following table:

| $f(x,y)$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=3$ | $Y=4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $\dfrac{1}{8}$ | $\dfrac{1}{8}$ | $\dfrac{1}{8}$ | $\dfrac{1}{8}$ |
| $X=1$ | $\dfrac{1}{8}$ | $\dfrac{1}{8}$ | $\dfrac{1}{8}$ | $\dfrac{1}{8}$ |

Similar to the case of single random variables, we have

$$
f(x,y) = P(X=x\:\textrm{ and }\:Y=y).
$$

34343} {:db/id 17592186163076 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163328 :tutorial/content "Let $X$ and $Y$ be discrete random variables with supports $S_X$ and $S_Y$, respectively. For a function 

$$
f(x,y)=P(X=x, Y=y)
$$

 

to be a valid joint probability mass function with joint support $S=S_X\times S_Y,$ it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $0 \leq f(x,y) \leq 1$ for all $(x,y) \in S$

- $\displaystyle\sum\limits_{(x,y) \in S} f(x,y)= 1$

- $P\left((X,Y) \in A \right) = \displaystyle \sum\limits_{(x,y) \in A} f(x,y),$ where $A$ is a subset of $S.$

There is some nice intuition to these conditions.

- The condition $0 \leq f(x,y) \leq 1$ for all $(x,y)\in S$ states that any possible outcome for $(X,Y)$ must have a probability between $0$ and $1.$

- The condition $\displaystyle \sum\limits_{(x,y) \in S} f(x,y) = 1$ states that the sum of all the probabilities over all possible values of $X$ and $Y$ must add up to $1.$

- The third condition states that we compute the probability of an event $A$ by adding up the probabilities associated with $A.$

The joint probability mass function of a discrete random variable with finite support can be represented using a table, as shown below.

|  | $Y=y_1$ | $Y=y_2$ | $\ldots$ | $Y=y_n$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=x_1$ | $f(x_1,y_1)$ | $f(x_1,y_2)$ | $\ldots$ | $f(x_1,y_n)$ |
| $X=x_2$ | $f(x_2,y_1)$ | $f(x_2,y_2)$ | $\ldots$ | $f(x_2,y_n)$ |
| $\ldots$ | $\ldots$ | $\ldots$ | $\ldots$ | $\ldots$ |
| $X=x_k$ | $f(x_k,y_1)$ | $f(x_k,y_2)$ | $\ldots$ | $f(x_k,y_n)$ |

In the case of two random variables, the joint distribution is sometimes called a **bivariate distribution**.
However, the concept generalizes to any number of random variables, giving a **multivariate distribution**." :tutorial/id #uuid "5f5858f9-f1f3-5d98-b436-9ffd034a3e9d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6284 :tutorial/title "Bivariate and Multivariate Distributions"} :step/id #uuid "2636297d-b114-590c-9454-08ebab970ce2" :step/math-academy-id 38084 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162982}}] :activity/title "Joint Distributions for Discrete Random Variables" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186162162} {:db/id 17592186162952 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163262 :tutorial/content "We often want to know if there is a relationship between two random variables. For this reason, we wish to formulate the idea of a joint probability distribution.

To introduce this concept, suppose the random variable $X$ represents the number of heads obtained when a fair coin is flipped. The support of $X,$ denoted $S_X,$ consists of all possible values of $X$ and in this case is given by

$$
S_X = \{0,1\}.
$$

Now suppose that the random variable $Y$ represents the result of rolling a fair tetrahedral die. Then the support of $Y,$ denoted $S_Y,$ is

$$
S_Y = \{1,2,3,4\}.
$$

The **joint support** of $X$ and $Y,$ denoted $S,$ consists of all possible pairs $(x,y)$ such that $x$ is a possible outcome for $X$ and $y$ is a possible outcome for $Y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(0,1), & (0,2), & (0,3), & (0,4) \\ (1,1), & (1,2), & (1,3), & (1,4)\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $S_X\times S_Y$ is the cartesian product of $S_X$ and $S_Y.$

A **joint probability distribution** is a probability distribution over a set of pairs [math](X, Y),[/math] where [math]X[/math] and [math]Y[/math] are both random variables. In this lesson, we will focus on the case where [math]X[/math] and [math]Y[/math] are *discrete* random variables, in which case the joint probability distribution is called a **joint probability mass function**. 

Let's assume that the flipping of the coin and rolling of the die are independent. Then, for any $x \in X$ and any $y \in Y,$ we have that

$$
P(X=x\:\textrm{and}\:Y=y) = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1}{8}.
$$

 

The **joint probability mass function** of $X$ and $Y,$ denoted $f(x,y),$ can be represented by the following table:

| $f(x,y)$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=3$ | $Y=4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $\dfrac{1}{8}$ | $\dfrac{1}{8}$ | $\dfrac{1}{8}$ | $\dfrac{1}{8}$ |
| $X=1$ | $\dfrac{1}{8}$ | $\dfrac{1}{8}$ | $\dfrac{1}{8}$ | $\dfrac{1}{8}$ |

Similar to the case of single random variables, we have

$$
f(x,y) = P(X=x\:\textrm{ and }\:Y=y).
$$

Going forward, we will use the shorthand notation $P(X=x, Y=y)$ to mean $P(X=x\:\textrm{ and }\:Y=y).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "79b99576-5a28-5c03-bc5d-1cc472ef0795" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5348 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "9628dc39-75f0-5169-a945-48c68e6e4f31" :step/math-academy-id 33477 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163076}} {:db/id 17592186163262 :tutorial/content "We often want to know if there is a relationship between two random variables. $$
A \times B = \big\{(a, b) \: : \: a \in A,\, b \in B \big\}
$$

Many Cartesian products have natural representations in the Cartesian plane. The most common of these is the Cartesian product $\mathbb R^2{:}$

$$
\mathbb R^2 = \mathbb R\times\mathbb R =  \big\{(x, y) \: : \: x,y \in \mathbb R \big\}
$$

This infinite set contains all ordered pairs $(x,y),$ where $x$ and $y$ can be any real numbers. In other words, $\mathbb R^2$ contains every point in the Cartesian plane! 

![](images/07/070389fcdb6d69f9aa90dabbd98a0d3461e26d3e3e08b1d53b92e99688c09923.png)

Similarly, the set

$$
\mathbb R^3 = \mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R =  \big\{(x, y, z) \: : \: x,y,z \in \mathbb R \big\}
$$

describes every point in three-dimensional Cartesian space. 

![](images/e7/e74fb5948144bc61173e4de73865cb746278bd31fd87e4abf927fa01821ba936.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "c18e6618-573b-5560-8d95-58ed56f05155" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8237 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c7652427-e5ff-5d02-9f23-39039f090aff" :step/math-academy-id 153383 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199078}} {:db/id 17592186199078 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198272 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198169 :question/id #uuid "bb40c174-3739-50df-835e-5d47c9902d5b" :question/math-academy-id "e-13192"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c3a2b291-c6dd-58c8-a10f-d851511d7bfc" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048899} {:db/id 17592186050367} {:db/id 17592186050432} {:db/id 17592186050763} {:db/id 17592186050923}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198802} {:db/id 17592186198807} {:db/id 17592186287775} {:db/id 17592186287870} {:db/id 17592186287871} {:db/id 17592186389895} {:db/id 17592186390326} {:db/id 17592186421830}] :knowledge-point/title "Sketching Cartesian Products in the Coordinate Plane"} :step/id #uuid "2190f1df-5853-5d8c-85e2-33f40f1f0f24" :step/math-academy-id 153384 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199079}} {:db/id 17592186199079 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199579 :tutorial/content "Cartesian coordinates can also be used to visualize other Cartesian products.

For example, let's consider the following Cartesian product:

$$
\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^- = \big\{(x,y) \: : \: x\in\mathbb N,\, y\in\mathbb R^-\big\}
$$

This product contains every point in $\mathbb R^2$ whose $x$-coordinate is a natural number and whose $y$-coordinate is a negative real number.

To visualize this Cartesian product, consider the following subset of our Cartesian product:

$$
S_1 = \big\{ (1,y) \: : \: y \in\mathbb{R}^- \big\} \subset \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^-
$$

This subset describes all points in the plane whose $x$-coordinate equals $1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any negative real number. We can represent $S_1$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/f6/f6165f66b4149b7b2ea52a3cd686836853d85048ca890e850cb771174a150c57.png)

Next, we consider the subset $S_2,$ given by

$$
S_2 = \big\{ (2,y) \: : \: y \in\mathbb{R}^- \big\} \subset \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^-.
$$

This subset describes all points in the plane whose $x$-coordinate equals $2$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any negative real number. 

![](images/ca/caf2299a2e8009ad5b2776ce67786fa7c7e3bdb57aacbd7df87882f59a2350e2.png)

We can create the subsets $S_3, S_4, S_5,\ldots,$ similarly. Our Cartesian product consists of the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}N\times {R}^{-} & ={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}\cup ⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^-$ as the set of vertical rays shown in the diagram below.

17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186198532} {:db/id 17592186199077 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199560 :tutorial/content "Recall that if $A$ and $B$ are sets, the Cartesian product $A \times B$ consists of all ordered pairs $(a,b)$ whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A \times B = \big\{(a, b) \: : \: a \in A,\, b \in B \big\}
$$

Many Cartesian products have natural representations in the Cartesian plane. The most common of these is the Cartesian product $\mathbb R^2{:}$

$$
\mathbb R^2 = \mathbb R\times\mathbb R =  \big\{(x, y) \: : \: x,y \in \mathbb R \big\}
$$

This infinite set contains all ordered pairs $(x,y),$ where $x$ and $y$ can be any real numbers. In other words, $\mathbb R^2$ contains every point in the Cartesian plane! 

![](images/07/070389fcdb6d69f9aa90dabbd98a0d3461e26d3e3e08b1d53b92e99688c09923.png)

Similarly, the set

$$
\mathbb R^3 = \mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R =  \big\{(x, y, z) \: : \: x,y,z \in \mathbb R \big\}
$$

describes every point in three-dimensional Cartesian space.

For example, let's consider the following Cartesian product:

$$
\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^- = \big\{(x,y) \: : \: x\in\mathbb N,\, y\in\mathbb R^-\big\}
$$

This product contains every point in $\mathbb R^2$ whose $x$-coordinate is a natural number and whose $y$-coordinate is a negative real number.

To visualize this Cartesian product, consider the following subset of our Cartesian product:

$$
S_1 = \big\{ (1,y) \: : \: y \in\mathbb{R}^- \big\} \subset \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^-
$$

This subset describes all points in the plane whose $x$-coordinate equals $1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any negative real number. We can represent $S_1$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/f6/f6165f66b4149b7b2ea52a3cd686836853d85048ca890e850cb771174a150c57.png)

Next, we consider the subset $S_2,$ given by

$$
S_2 = \big\{ (2,y) \: : \: y \in\mathbb{R}^- \big\} \subset \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^-.
$$

This subset describes all points in the plane whose $x$-coordinate equals $2$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any negative real number. 

![](images/ca/caf2299a2e8009ad5b2776ce67786fa7c7e3bdb57aacbd7df87882f59a2350e2.png)

We can create the subsets $S_3, S_4, S_5,\ldots,$ similarly. Our Cartesian product consists of the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}N\times {R}^{-} & ={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}\cup ⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}^-$ as the set of vertical rays shown in the diagram below.

"95207fcf-4f1f-5c3f-a008-9c15baaebacc" :topic/math-academy-id 3002} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186162990 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163281 :tutorial/content "The joint PMF $f(x,y)$ of two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ tells us all possible events $(X, Y)$ and the probabilities associated with each event. However, suppose we wish to determine the probability mass function for $X$ only. How can this be deduced from the joint PMF?

Let's build some intuition by considering an example.

Consider the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y,$ shown below.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X={\color{blue}{1}}$ | $0.05$ | $0.15$ |
| $X={\color{red}{2}}$ | $0.7$ | $0.1$ |

The support of $X$ is $S_X = \{{\color{blue}{1}},{\color{red}{2}}\}.$ Let's now deduce the probabilities associated with each value of $X$ in $S_X\mathbin{:}$

- According to the law of total probability, we can deduce $P(X=1)$ by summing the values in the first row of the table, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=1) & =P(X=1,Y=1)+P(X=1,Y=2) \\  & =0.05+0.15 \\  & =0.2\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we summed over all possible values of $Y$ associated with $X=1.$

- Similarly, by summing the values in the second row in the table, we have

$$

:tutorial/content "Let's go back to the last example for the random variables $X$ and $Y.$

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.05$ | $0.15$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.7$ | $0.1$ |

We saw that the marginal mass function $f_X$ for $X$ is found by summing the rows in the table. So let's add the sum of each row to our table:

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | $f_X$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.05$ | $0.15$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0.2}$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.7$ | $0.1$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0.8}$ |

Notice how we wrote the values of the *marginal* mass function in the right *margin* of the table.

From here, we can immediately deduce that 

$$
P(X=1) = f_X(1) = 0.2, \qquad P(X=2) = f_X(2) = 0.8.
$$

Similarly, we can compute the marginal mass function of $Y,$ denoted $f_Y(y),$ by summing the columns. Adding these totals to our table, we get the following:

| $f$ | $Y={\color{blue}{1}}$ | $Y={\color{red}{2}}$ | $f_X$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.05$ | $0.15$ | $0.2$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.7$ | $0.1$ | $0.8$ |
| $f_Y$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0.75}$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0.25}$ | $1$ |

Again, notice how we wrote the values of the *marginal* mass function in the bottom *margin* of the table.

From here, we can immediately deduce that 

$$
P(Y={\color{blue}{1}}) = f_Y({\color{blue}{1}}) = 0.75, \qquad P(Y={\color{red}{2}}) = f_Y({\color{red}{2}}) = 0.25.
$$

Finally, the marginal mass function $f_Y(y)$ of $Y$ is as follows:

| $y$ | $\color{blue}1$ | $\color{red}2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f_Y(y)$ | $0.75$ | $0.25$ |" :tutorial/id #uuid "a1c9ecf8-619b-58b7-899f-b179dca8ae45" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6290 :tutorial/title "Deducing the Marginal Mass Function for Y"} :step/id #uuid "83e1320a-f77b-5173-bedf-f02c9d400247" :step/math-academy-id 38105 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163083}} {:db/id 17592186163083 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163332 :tutorial/content "Now that we've built some intuition, let's define the marginal mass functions formally.

Let $f(x,y)$ be the joint PMF of the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with supports $S_X$ and $S_Y$, respectively.

- The **marginal mass function ** of $X,$ denoted $f_X(x),$ is defined as

$$
f_X(x) = P(X=x)  = \displaystyle \sum\limits_{y \in S_Y} f(x,y).
$$

- The **marginal mass function ** of $Y,$ denoted $f_Y(y),$ is defined as

$$
f_Y(y)= P(Y=y)  = \displaystyle \sum\limits_{x \in S_X} f(x,y).
$$

We can relate these definitions to our previous intuition:

- The first definition states that, to compute $P(X=x)$ for some particular value $x,$ we sum all possible values of $Y$ in the row corresponding to $X=x.$

- The second definition states that, to compute $P(Y=y)$ for some particular value $y,$ we sum all possible values of $X$ in the column corresponding to $Y=y.$

Finally, note that marginal mass functions are sometimes called **marginal probability mass functions**, **marginal PMFs**, or (less formally) **marginal distributions**." :tutorial/id #uuid "ddca7e0f-a315-5567-97d7-f5b40876617b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6291 :tutorial/title "A Formal Definition of the Marginal Mass Function"} :step/id #uuid "97117126-1ac4-57aa-9c23-c3e882c06372" :step/math-academy-id 38106 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162997}}] :activity/title "Marginal Distributions for Discrete Random Variables" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186162163} {:db/id 17592186162990 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163281 :tutorial/content "The joint PMF $f(x,y)$ of two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ tells us all possible events $(X, Y)$ and the probabilities associated with each event. However, suppose we wish to determine the probability mass function for $X$ only. How can this be deduced from the joint PMF?

Let's build some intuition by considering an example.

Consider the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y,$ shown below.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X={\color{blue}{1}}$ | $0.05$ | $0.15$ |
| $X={\color{red}{2}}$ | $0.7$ | $0.1$ |

The support of $X$ is $S_X = \{{\color{blue}{1}},{\color{red}{2}}\}.$ Let's now deduce the probabilities associated with each value of $X$ in $S_X\mathbin{:}$

- According to the law of total probability, we can deduce $P(X=1)$ by summing the values in the first row of the table, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=1) & =P(X=1,Y=1)+P(X=1,Y=2) \\  & =0.05+0.15 \\  & =0.2\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we summed over all possible values of $Y$ associated with $X=1.$

- Similarly, by summing the values in the second row in the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=2) & =P(X=2,Y=1)+P(X=2,Y=2) \\  & =0.7+0.1 \\  & =0.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we summed over all possible values of $Y$ associated with $X=2.$

Therefore, the probability mass function for $X$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $\color{blue}1$ | $\color{red}2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f_X(x)$ | $0.2$ | $0.8$ |

Notice that we have used the notation $f_X(x).$ Since $f_X(x)$ was deduced from the joint probability mass function $f(x,y),$ we call $f_X(x)$ the **marginal mass function** for $X.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "0281a245-2f6d-5a89-8ea7-5d77bf3dca4f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5469 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0dce6d66-b5fe-52cc-ae58-8918d96eb144" :step/math-academy-id 34052 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163082}} {:db/id 17592186163281 :tutorial/content "The joint PMF $f(x,y)$ of two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ tells us all possible events $(X, Y)$ and the probabilities associated with each event. The support of $X$ is $S_X = \{{\color{blue}{1}},{\color{red}{2}}\}.$ Let's now deduce the probabilities associated with each value of $X$ in $S_X\mathbin{:}$

- According to the law of total probability, we can deduce $P(X=1)$ by summing the values in the first row of the table, as follows:

- $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x$ in $S$

- $\displaystyle \int_{S} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 1$

It is common for the set $S$ of a continuous random variable $X$ to be an infinite interval. Therefore, we often need to evaluate improper integrals when determining whether a function is a valid pdf and to compute probabilities associated with such a random variable.

For example, let's consider the following function:

![](images/38/38ea105f5dd0cea7784bf73f814e7161b90cfd224eb099084cc33b6539d95fdd.svg)

Is $f(x)$ a valid probability density function? Let's start by sketching its graph:

:question/math-academy-id "q-87226" :question/problem "Compute $P(X>3)$ given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{{x}^{5}},\, & x\ge 1, \\ 0,\, & x<1.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "If a continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x),$ then 

$$
P(a<X<b)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, in our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>3) & =P(3\le X<\infty ) \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{\infty }\frac{4}{{x}^{5}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}]}_{3}^{\infty } \\  & =\frac{1}{81}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1be2574c-a3ce-5ec0-bb9f-88e4dc8755a2" :step/next {:db/id 17592186421867}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "28308daa-8ddb-545e-8465-8f0a73db0af6" :answer/type {:db/id The **extreme value theorem** answers this question and states the following:

> *If $f(x)$ is a continuous function defined on the closed interval $[a,b],$ then $f(x)$ always has at least one global maximum and one global minimum on $[a,b]$*.

For example, consider the function $f(x),$ given by

$$
f(x) = (x-3)^2, \qquad x\in [2,5].
$$

Notice that this function satisfies the conditions for the extreme value theorem:

- the function $f(x)$ is *continuous* on the interval $x\in [2,5]$, and

- the interval $[2,5]$ is *closed*.

Since *both* conditions are satisfied, the extreme value theorem guarantees that $f(x)$ must have at least one global maximum and one global minimum.

To see that this is indeed true, let's sketch the graph of $f(x).$ 

![](images/d2/d2ceffc40ead80b03d73004b663b91a942444bd14ce9e1e68fc98ffebbae3423.png)

From the diagram, we see that the function $f(x)$ has 

- a global maximum at $x=5,$ and

- a global minimum at $x=3.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "300a3bb8-a79f-5387-8c5e-1e403c2df531" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2666 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid $$

$$

Notice that $g(x)$ is defined on a semi-open interval (the right endpoint is open). As a result, we cannot guarantee that $g(x)$ has a global maximum and a global minimum.

![](images/a7/a7648d89fc02372f8d48a649425fa5dba4c8a86e12e9fa7bbddc69ffe52575c3.png)

$$
{\begin{aligned}(x-3)^{2}, & \,2\le x<3, \\ (x-3)^{2}+1, & \,3\le x\le 5.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $h(x)$ is defined on the closed interval $[2,5].$ However, since $h(x)$ is not continuous on $[2,5],$ we cannot guarantee that $h(x)$ has both a global maximum and minimum on $[2,5].$

of a 2x2 Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "8cbda370-20f2-5e6b-9780-b0122e4ee2a0" :step/math-academy-id 20166} {:db/id 17592186176678 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176975 :tutorial/content "Let's find the eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-\textrm{i}$ of the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-\textrm{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} & -1 \\ 2 & -1+\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(1+\text{i}){x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+(-1+\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-\textrm{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another.

As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
x_2 = (1+\textrm{i})x_1.
$$

Therefore, by setting $x_1\in\mathbb C$ to be the free variable, we find that the general solution to our system is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (1+\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}]
$$

Setting $x_1=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that our eigenvector has complex-valued entries.

**Note:** To check our result, we can show that $A\mathbf v = \lambda \mathbf v.$ Computing $A\mathbf v,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1-\text{i}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and computing $\lambda \mathbf v$ gives

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}]
$$

So $A\mathbf v = \lambda \mathbf v,$ as required." :tutorial/id #uuid "1bde3a85-d8df-5194-8581-77fe2108627c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4297 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "8f4ddd6c-a17e-54f3-bade-a64685e04b36" :step/math-academy-id 26123 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176644}}] :activity/title "Finding Complex Eigenvectors of Real 2x2 Matrices" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186176123} {:db/id 17592186176678 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176975 :tutorial/content "Let's find the eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-\textrm{i}$ of the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]$

what is the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 8 \\ -2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-(-2)(8) & =0 \\ 1-2\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +17 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{2\pm \sqrt{(-2)^{2}-4(1)(17)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{2\pm \sqrt{-64}}{2} \\  & =\frac{2\pm 8\text{i}}{2} \\  & =1\pm 4\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =1\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1+4\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1+4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 1+4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4\text{i} & 8 \\ -2 & -4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-4\text{i}{x}_{1}+8{x}_{2}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}-4\text{i}{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(1+4\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}\text{i}{x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ \frac{1}{2}\text{i}{x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=2,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ \text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=1-4\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$

:question/math-academy-id "q-140388" :question/problem "Given that ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}],$
what is the value of $\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & 4 \\ -5 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (7-\lambda )(3-\lambda )-(4)(-5) & =0 \\ 21-7\lambda -3\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+20 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +41 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{-(-10)\pm \sqrt{(-10)^{2}-4(1)(41)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{-(-10)\pm \sqrt{-64}}{2} \\  & =\frac{10\pm 8\text{i}}{2} \\  & =5\pm 4\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =5\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5+4\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5+4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 5+4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-4\text{i} & 4 \\ -5 & -2-4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(2-4\text{i}){x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}+(-2-4\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(5+4\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}(-2-4\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}(-2-4\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2+4\text{i} \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=5-4\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2-4\text{i} \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-5)(-5)}{(2+4\text{i})(2-4\text{i})}=\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d4502c0c-e4ff-5fb4-9162-5b78360320c6"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "006f21ef-bd9e-5319-853e-7e3fc38e4a67" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\lambda $$

Since $Av=7\text{i}v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =7\text{i}.$"} :step/id #uuid "db758ac7-852d-51b4-ad30-e5acef4cfcd0" :step/next :tutorial/content "Let's look again at the graph of the function $y=\cos x.$ 

![](images/88/88378ece5b1721cdc533d07d69c004901539c7f8fda9a5a3e5c5648ed32905c5.png)

The cosine function has infinitely many zeros and an infinite number of points where the function reaches its maximum and minimum value. Let's write general expressions for these properties, assuming $n$ is an integer.

**The Zeros of the Function**

From the graph, we see that the zeros of the function are $x=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pm \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\dots$ 

A general expression for the zeros is

$$
x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + n\pi.
$$

**The Maxima of the Function**

The function has a maximum when $x=0$ and is periodic with period $2\pi.$ Therefore, a general expression for the values of $x$ that maximize cosine is

$$
x = 2n\pi.
$$

**The Minima of the Function**

The function has a minimum when $x=\pi$ and is periodic with period $2\pi.$ Therefore, a general expression for the values of $x$ that minimize cosine is

$$
x = \pi + 2n\pi.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "46e10740-fb99-59c2-8277-45bf39d4988e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6896 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "96434733-6b0d-57f8-b32a-6d08028990e9" :step/math-academy-id 41780 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176856}} {:db/id 17592186176856 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176047 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175693 :question/id #uuid "70569afd-42c4-5e5f-8397-4fbd873eb8e4" :question/math-academy-id "e-11002"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "542df339-5020-5680-a39c-a1ae161083e7" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050033} {:db/id 17592186050718}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186176448} {:db/id 17592186176449} {:db/id 17592186235452} {:db/id 17592186237982} {:db/id 17592186237983} {:db/id 17592186292696} {:db/id 17592186338799} {:db/id 17592186338800}] :knowledge-point/title "Describing Properties of the Cosine Function"} :step/id #uuid "917ddcd7-bc4f-5e36-8f78-dd85b3ecbfe5" :step/math-academy-id 41781 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176857}} {:db/id 17592186176857 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177065 :tutorial/content "Let's look at the graph of the cosine function again.

![](images/04/04f13f2dec860874174f51990f4260615e7be893a6be5f86b3b13857c4e8953f.png)

The periodicity of the function is another characteristic of its graph. The period of the cosine function is $2\pi,$ shown below:

![](images/78/789fa06939a3e3350a18c4e9cdf078bf6baf3f025709703e608cb3b7ba89e698.png)

This means that $\cos\left( x+2n\pi\right) = \cos \left( x\right)$ for any number $x$ and any integer $n.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5cc2e21c-1a75-53dd-85be-61d9124f25c6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6897 :tutorial/title "The Periodicity Property of the Cosine Function"} :step/id #uuid "95d7359c-3367-567b-8a0b-4546d0d324da" :step/math-academy-id 41784 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176858}} {:db/id 17592186176858 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176048 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175694 :question/id #uuid "a8cc8b8f-463b-5734-a33d-e915159cba32" :question/math-academy-id "e-11003"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1c25c3a0-083a-55d5-b688-7347bfafaa9e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049353}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186176546} {:db/id 17592186176547} {:db/id 17592186237984} {:db/id 17592186237985} {:db/id 17592186237986} {:db/id 17592186338802} {:db/id 17592186338803}] :knowledge-point/title "Utilizing the Periodicity Property of the Cosine Function"} :step/id #uuid "fdae8229-a567-5401-adbc-7dc3c17d7b91" :step/math-academy-id 41785 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176895}} {:db/id 17592186176875 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176057 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175703 :question/id #uuid "08253dde-510a-5451-ba5c-64d42d647db2" :question/math-academy-id "e-11012"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "94645507-186a-54a7-a96b-ccfb0fb1f769" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049873}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186176346} {:db/id 17592186176355} {:db/id 17592186269129} {:db/id 17592186275428} {:db/id 17592186275430} {:db/id 17592186275434}] :knowledge-point/title "Utilizing the Evenness Property of the Cosine Function"} :step/id #uuid "763338f7-5348-5442-87d5-00b41679ebf8" :step/math-academy-id 41829} {:db/id 17592186176895 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177082 :tutorial/content "Recall that a function $f(x)$ is *even* if it satisfies the property

$$
f(-x) = f(x).
$$

As it turns out, cosine is an even function! So, for any value of $x,$ we have

$$
\cos(-x) = \cos(x).
$$

Even functions are always symmetric about the $y$-axis. This is indeed true of the cosine function, as we can see from the diagram below. 

![](images/b1/b1f44126ba6188d147026b6fe5a4066b0051ec3b638bb2d3e34ee1cbb1708cae.png)

We can use the evenness property of cosine in conjunction with its periodicity property to simplify trigonometric expressions. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "c7ca8a70-b8fa-5e67-adec-ee263651a473" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7897 :tutorial/title "The Evenness Property of the Cosine Function"} :step/id #uuid "5a441a39-9db7-5be4-8b0d-dbbb978a8599" :step/math-academy-id 45521 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176875}}] :activity/title "Describing Properties of the Cosine Function" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186176108} {:db/id 17592186176855 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177064 :tutorial/content "Let's look again at the graph of the function $y=\cos x.$

The function has a maximum when $x=0$ and is periodic with period $2\pi.$ Therefore, a general expression for the values of $x$ that maximize cosine is

The function has a minimum when $x=\pi$ and is periodic with period $2\pi.$ Therefore, a general expression for the values of $x$ that minimize cosine is

$$

$$
f(-x) = f(x).
$$

As it turns out, cosine is an even function! So, for any value of $x,$ we have

$$
\cos(-x) = \cos(x).
$$

Even functions are always symmetric about the $y$-axis. This is indeed true of the cosine function, as we can see from the diagram below. 

![](images/b1/b1f44126ba6188d147026b6fe5a4066b0051ec3b638bb2d3e34ee1cbb1708cae.png)

We can use the evenness property of cosine in conjunction with its periodicity property to simplify trigonometric expressions. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "c7ca8a70-b8fa-5e67-adec-ee263651a473" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7897 :tutorial/title "The Evenness Property of the Cosine Function"} :step/id #uuid "5a441a39-9db7-5be4-8b0d-dbbb978a8599" :step/math-academy-id 45521 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176875}} {:db/id 17592186176875 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176057 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175703 :question/id #uuid "08253dde-510a-5451-ba5c-64d42d647db2" :question/math-academy-id "e-11012"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "94645507-186a-54a7-a96b-ccfb0fb1f769" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049873}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186176346} {:db/id 17592186176355} {:db/id 17592186269129} {:db/id 17592186275428} {:db/id 17592186275430} {:db/id 17592186275434}] :knowledge-point/title "Utilizing the Evenness Property of the Cosine Function"} :step/id #uuid "763338f7-5348-5442-87d5-00b41679ebf8" :step/math-academy-id 41829} {:db/id 17592186177082 :tutorial/content "Recall that a function $f(x)$ is *even* if it satisfies the property

$$
x=\big\{ x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_n \big\}, \qquad 
y=\big\{ y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n \big\},
$$

the **covariance** between $x$ and $y,$ denoted by $\textrm{Cov}(x,y),$ is a measure that evaluates the extent to which $x$ and $y$ change together.

- A positive covariance means that if $x$ increases, then $y$ is also likely to increase:

![](images/bb/bbfae3f0fb38bc8652cd26716e4b0b128cf1f2039350267034d97161d7f5dac4.png)

- A negative covariance means that if $x$ increases, then $y$ is likely to decrease:

![](images/fd/fd45053fdc39f070e3438c3b8c61fe01613201595cfe00bd4cc6c6e481bf73ab.png)

- A covariance of zero (or close to zero) indicates that there is no *linear* relationship between $x$ and $y.$

![](images/a5/a58fa4d40d77af23df86b5bd8eaca3119b93bc9ea97cc435eb4e53ba2777b071.png)

**Watch Out!** A covariance of zero does *not* mean that $x$ and $y$ are not related. It simply means the relationship between them is not linear. To illustrate, consider the image below.

![](images/a4/a4bdbf92e691174644dda9b9a84acb1b896c0436afb221501dc10b4635841539.png)

The (nonlinear) relationship shown above is $y=x^2.$ However, it can be shown that $\textrm{Cov}(x,y) = 0$ for this data set.

To calculate $\textrm{Cov}(x,y),$ we use the following formula: 

$$
\textrm{Cov}(x,y) =  \dfrac{1}{n} \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})(y_i - \overline{y}),
$$

where $\overline{x}$  and $\overline{y}$ denote the means of $x$ and $y$ respectively.

**Note**: This formula for the covariance assumes that $x$ and $y$ are drawn from a *population*. There is a slightly different formula for covariance when $x$ and $y$ are sample data. However, we won't worry about the difference for now." :tutorial/id #uuid "da03b3e7-b452-59b9-b81e-5dd75cea02a2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10301 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid The (population) covariance of the data sets

$$
x=\big\{ x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_n \big\}, \qquad

$$

$$

- The **conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y$,** denoted $f_{X|Y}(x|y),$ is defined as $$f_{X|Y}(x|y) = P(X = x \,|\, Y = y) = \dfrac{P(X = x, \, Y = y)}{P(Y=y)} = \dfrac{f(x,y)}{f_Y(y)},$$ where $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and $f_Y(y)$ is the marginal mass function of $Y.$

- The **conditional probability mass function of $Y$ given that $X=x,$** denoted $f_{Y|X}(y|x),$ is defined as $$f_{Y|X}(y|x) = P(Y = y \,|\, X = x) = \dfrac{P(X = x,\, Y = y)}{P(X=x)} = \dfrac{f(x,y)}{f_X(x)},$$ where $f(x,y)$ is a joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and $f_X(x)$ is the marginal mass function of $X.$

**Watch out!** The conditional distribution of $X$ given $Y$ does *not* equal the conditional distribution of $Y$ given $X$. That is, in general,

$$f_{X|Y}(x|y) \ne f_{Y|X}(y|x).$$

Finally, if $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then

$$f_{X|Y}(x|y)=f_X(x),\qquad f_{Y|X}(y|x)=f_Y(y).$$

In other words, if $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then knowing the value of one random variable does not affect the probability distribution of the other." :tutorial/id #uuid "1cbdc2c5-105c-5f9a-b4f4-7e4651bdc789" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6273 :tutorial/title "Conditional Probability Mass Functions"} :step/id #uuid "acc71c94-7794-57f0-bfff-16c3d8ed9e31" :step/math-academy-id 38019 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163066}}] :activity/title "Conditional Distributions for Discrete Random Variables" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186162164} {:db/id 17592186163004 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163288 :tutorial/content "Let's recall the multiplication law for conditional probability for two events ![](images/32/3207697e43e4f88223ad85c16964c3103a50c0c999a4ca14417695158d45526b.svg) and ![](images/5d/5d8b650b90c85fbc0db5e4b6fae61767e293a843d18a2526f3ee4157733e1f4b.svg) ![](images/44/44229a2a35108e36c1348009a552be50e798af9b2807f49c4e4ef8515ed7eefe.svg)

- The **conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y$,** denoted $f_{X|Y}(x|y),$ is defined as $$f_{X|Y}(x|y) = P(X = x \,|\, Y = y) = \dfrac{P(X = x, \, Y = y)}{P(Y=y)} = \dfrac{f(x,y)}{f_Y(y)},$$ where $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and $f_Y(y)$ is the marginal mass function of $Y.$

- The **conditional probability mass function of $Y$ given that $X=x,$** denoted $f_{Y|X}(y|x),$ is defined as $$f_{Y|X}(y|x) = P(Y = y \,|\, X = x) = \dfrac{P(X = x,\, Y = y)}{P(X=x)} = \dfrac{f(x,y)}{f_X(x)},$$ where $f(x,y)$ is a joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and $f_X(x)$ is the marginal mass function of $X.$

**Watch out!** The conditional distribution of $X$ given $Y$ does *not* equal the conditional distribution of $Y$ given $X$. That is, in general,

$$f_{X|Y}(x|y) \ne f_{Y|X}(y|x).$$

Finally, if $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then

$$f_{X|Y}(x|y)=f_X(x),\qquad f_{Y|X}(y|x)=f_Y(y).$$

In other words, if $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then knowing the value of one random variable does not affect the probability distribution of the other." :tutorial/id #uuid "1cbdc2c5-105c-5f9a-b4f4-7e4651bdc789" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6273 :tutorial/title "Conditional Probability Mass Functions"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046659} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186410519} :activity/id #uuid "4f58fa0a-3eab-578c-8ede-b29945f6d461" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049149 :topic/id #uuid "de945224-de03-5292-84ca-39d9ddf3f7e4" :topic/math-academy-id 3003} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186410516 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410515 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "36eae30e-fa0d-5135-a62d-0465c3393122" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186410485} {:answer/id #uuid "500b7039-9773-5a4d-a57b-2ec78d1c6cc4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{13}" :db/id 17592186410489} {:answer/id #uuid "568228f9-502e-5052-aae6-cf24f3f3e87c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{16}" :db/id 17592186410490} {:answer/id #uuid "7f2cbc96-2672-5c50-abb6-ff77349a1002" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186410495} {:answer/id #uuid "b71aacf7-31c6-5c18-bf8d-c7c655c001fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{13}" :db/id 17592186410496}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410489} :answer-field/id #uuid "b9630d02-fcc6-50aa-af4a-264fb35a6574" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410509}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b1e5d993-4954-596b-9a63-c575f6c7babb" :question/math-academy-id "q-142903" :question/problem "| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=3$ |

$$

Therefore, we're required to compute the conditional probability

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(3\,|\,3)=P(Y=3\,|\,X=3).
$$

By the multiplication law for conditional probability, we have

$$
P(Y=3\,|\,X=3)=\frac{P(X=3,Y=3)}{P(X=3)}=\frac{f(3,3)}{{f}_{X}(3)}
$$

where $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the marginal distribution of $X.$

Recall that the marginal distribution for $X$ corresponds to the row totals. Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(3) & =f(3,1)+f(3,2)+f(3,3) \\  & =\frac{5}{32}+\frac{5}{32}+\frac{3}{32} \\  & =\frac{13}{32}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given table, $f(3,3)=\frac{3}{32}.$ 

Finally, substituting  ${f}_{X}(3)=\frac{13}{32}$ and $f(3,3)=\frac{3}{32}$ in our formula above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(3\,|\,3) & =P(Y=3\,|\,X=3) \\  & =\frac{f(3,3)}{{f}_{X}(3)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{32})}{(\frac{13}{32})} \\  & =\frac{3}{13}.\end{aligned}

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=P(Y=y\,|\,X=x).
$$

Therefore, we're required to compute the following set of conditional probabilities:

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,3)=P(Y=y\,|\,X=3)
$$

By the multiplication law for conditional probability, we have

$$
P(Y=y\,|\,X=3)=\frac{P(X=3,Y=y)}{P(X=3)}=\frac{f(3,y)}{{f}_{X}(3)}
$$

where $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the marginal distribution of $X.$

Recall that the marginal distributions for $X$ and $Y$ correspond to the row and column totals, respectively. So, let's compute these:

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=3$ | ${f}_{X}(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.15$ | $0.2$ | $0.05$ | $0.4$ |
| $X=3$ | $0.4$ | $0.1$ | $0.1$ | $0.6$ |
| ${f}_{Y}(y)$ | $0.55$ | $0.3$ | $0.15$ | $1$ |

Therefore, for $y\in {1,2,3},$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y=1\,|\,X=3) & =\frac{f(3,1)}{{f}_{X}(3)}=\frac{0.4}{0.6}=\frac{2}{3} \\ P(Y=2\,|\,X=3) & =\frac{f(3,2)}{{f}_{X}(3)}=\frac{0.1}{0.6}=\frac{1}{6} \\ P(Y=3\,|\,X=3) & =\frac{f(3,3)}{{f}_{X}(3)}=\frac{0.1}{0.6}=\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the conditional probability mass function can be represented by the following table:   

| $y$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,3)$ | $\frac{2}{3}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ |"} :step/id #uuid "30942c86-dbc3-5faa-928f-8a3e27c6ef2a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186410520}} {:db/id 17592186410518 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410514 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1dea9c6c-8a37-5b15-a053-45fd4f8d2f9f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.6" :db/id 17592186410483} {:answer/id #uuid "c3b9f3ed-06e4-59ef-8471-d8398ce14731" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.25" :db/id 17592186410497} {:answer/id #uuid "d82990b6-7322-5310-a01d-936be990fc20" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5" :db/id 17592186410501} {:answer/id #uuid "f4c7c149-9c87-52d8-aaf5-4888360f519e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.4" :db/id 17592186410504} {:answer/id #uuid "f7a8127b-532b-5c4e-95ea-e82e38e362d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.75" :db/id 17592186410505}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410501} :answer-field/id #uuid "395c93a7-3493-526c-8001-2fe1cf196ffc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410507}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b172bfa5-07a0-5df8-8d2d-99d558ae1db4" :question/math-academy-id "q-142896" :question/problem "| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=3$ | $Y=5$ |
